The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

Assume AC and use the directional convention of
[[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. For probability measures $P,Q$ on one
measurable space, $D(P\|Q)\ge0$, and $D(P\|Q)=0$ if and only if $P=Q$.

There is also the following normalized-density identity. Let
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space: it is a set
with a sigma-algebra and measure ([[def-measure-space]]), and there is a
countable measurable cover by sets of finite $\mu$-measure
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]). Let
$\gamma:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable function with
$Z:=\int\gamma\,d\mu\in(0,\infty)$, and put $\pi=\gamma/Z$. Let
$q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable probability density,
so $\int q\,d\mu=1$, and suppose $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on
$\{\gamma=0\}$. Assume
$$\int q\bigl(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|\bigr)\,d\mu<\infty,$$
where each term with $q=0$ is defined to be zero. Then
$$\log Z =\int q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu +D(q\,\mu\|\pi\,\mu).$$
In particular, the first integral is at most $\log Z$. This identity concerns
normalized densities only; it does not assert posterior existence for an
unspecified statistical model.

derivations.claim: Let $g$ be the everywhere-positive Gaussian density in [F1] with mean $m$ and covariance $K$. Since $f$ is a Lebesgue density and $g>0$ everywhere, the law $P_f$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $P_g$. The log ratio is integrable: $\int f\ln f$ is finite by hypothesis, while $\ln g$ is a constant plus a quadratic form and $X$ has finite second moments. Hence $$D(P_f\|P_g)=\int f\ln(f/g)=-h(X)+\frac d2\ln(2\pi)+\frac12\ln\det K+\frac12\mathbb E[(X-m)^TK^{-1}(X-m)].$$ The last expectation is $\operatorname{tr}(K^{-1}K)=d$, by expanding the finite quadratic form and using the covariance entries.

By [F2], the left side in step 1.1 is nonnegative, which rearranges to the displayed entropy bound. Equality holds exactly when $D(P_f\|P_g)=0$, which by [F2] is equivalent to equality of the laws; thus $X\sim N_d(m,K)$. Conversely, substituting the density $g$ into the entropy integral gives equality because its centered quadratic expectation is $d$.

citations.quote: If $X$ has Lebesgue density $f$ on $\mathbb R^d$ and $\int f\ln f$ is a finite real number, its differential entropy in nats is $h(X):=-\int_{\mathbb R^d}f(x)\ln f(x)\,dx$. If $(X,S)$ has conditional densities $f_{X|S=s}$ for almost every $s$ and the indicated integral is finite, set $h(X|S):=\int h(f_{X|S=s})\,dP_S(s)$. We use only these finite-integral cases; differential entropy is not defined here by a formal subtraction of possibly infinite quantities.

derivations.claim: Let $q(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}e^{-|x|^2/2}$ and $M=\max\{1,\|f\|_\infty\}$. On $\{f>1\}$, $f\ln f\le f\ln M$, so the positive part is integrable. For $t\ge0$, $t\ln(1/t)\le1/e$; with $t=f/q$, this gives $f\ln(q/f)\le q/e$. Thus on $\{f\le1\}$, $$-f\ln f=f\ln(q/f)-f\ln q\le q/e+f|\ln q|.$$ The right side is integrable because $q$ is a probability density and $|\ln q|$ is bounded by a constant plus $|x|^2/2$. Hence the negative part of $f\ln f$ is integrable.
Both parts of $f\ln f$ are integrable by step 1.1. Therefore $\int f|\ln f|<\infty$, and [F1] defines a finite differential entropy.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a finite nonempty alphabet, let $P$ be a probability vector on $\mathcal A$ in the sense of [[def-qa-35-finite-probability-entropy-and-stochastic-matrices]], and let $n\ge1$. Write $\operatorname{supp}(P):=\{a\in\mathcal A:P(a)>0\}$. For $a^n=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in\mathcal A^n$, its empirical distribution is $\widehat P_{a^n}(a):=n^{-1}|\{t:a_t=a\}|$. For $\delta>0$, define the support-restricted strongly typical set by
$$T_\delta^{(n)}(P):=\{a^n\in\operatorname{supp}(P)^n:|\widehat P_{a^n}(a)-P(a)|\le\delta P(a)\text{ for every }a\text{ with }P(a)>0\}.$$
For a finite joint law $P_{XA}$ and a fixed $x^n$, write $T_\delta^{(n)}(P_{A|X}\mid x^n):=\{a^n:(x^n,a^n)\in T_\delta^{(n)}(P_{XA})\}$. This conditional set is empty if $x^n$ is outside the support of $P_X$. Zero-probability letters are excluded exactly, so no logarithm of zero occurs in likelihood calculations on these sets.

derivations.claim: Fix $a\in\mathcal A$ with $P(a)>0$, and set $B_i=\mathbf1_{\{X_i=a\}}$. The variables $B_i$ are IID Bernoulli with mean $P(a)$ and variance $P(a)(1-P(a))\le1/4$. Thus $\widehat P_{X^n}(a)=n^{-1}\sum_iB_i$ has mean $P(a)$ and variance at most $1/(4n)$. If $Z=\widehat P_{X^n}(a)-P(a)$, then pointwise $\mathbf1_{\{|Z|>\delta P(a)\}}\le Z^2/(\delta^2P(a)^2)$. Taking expectations bounds the deviation probability by $1/(4n\delta^2P(a)^2)$.

If $P(a)=0$, then $\Pr[X_i=a]=0$ for each $i$, so the probability that the word contains $a$ is zero by a finite union bound. There are finitely many positive-mass letters; summing the bounds from step 1.1 over them and adding the zero support event shows that the probability of failure of any condition in [F1] tends to zero.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

A **real scalar Gaussian relay network** has node set $[N]$ for an integer $N\ge1$, source set $\mathcal S\subseteq[N]$, destination set $\mathcal D\subseteq[N]$, one real input $X_i$ and output $Y_i$ at each node, and channel equations
$$Y_j=\sum_{i=1}^N g_{ji}X_i+Z_j,\qquad j\in[N],$$
where the gains $g_{ji}\in\mathbb R$ are fixed and the noises $Z_j$ are independent $N(0,1)$ random variables, independent across channel uses and of all source messages. At each use the current noise vector is independent of all past observations and the current inputs; future inputs may depend on past noises through feedback. Each node has a nonnegative power budget $P_i\ge0$ and average power constraint $\frac1n\sum_{t=1}^n\mathbb E[X_{i,t}^2]\le P_i$. Each source $i\in\mathcal S$ has an independent uniform message $M_i$ in a finite nonempty set $\mathcal M_i$. For every non-source node $i\notin\mathcal S$, set $\mathcal M_i=\{*\}$ and $M_i=*$, so its encoder has no message information. A length-$n$ causal code uses measurable encoders $X_{i,t}=f_{i,t}(M_i,Y_i^{t-1})$ and destination decoders based on $(Y_d^n,M_d)$, where $M_d$ is its own source message when $d\in\mathcal S$ and a singleton otherwise; multicast means every destination must decode every other source message, while its own message is already known. The average error probability is the probability that any required destination estimate is wrong. Write $G_{B,A}$ for the matrix with rows indexed by $B$ and columns by $A$ whose entries are $g_{ji}$.

Rates in this page's Gaussian formulas are measured in bits per use, $R_i=n^{-1}\log_2|\mathcal M_i|$.

All logarithms, mutual informations and rates in this lemma are in nats. Consider a memoryless network with finite node set $[N]$, source set $\mathcal S$, destination set $\mathcal D$, and independent uniform source messages, each required by every destination. Alphabets are either all finite, as in [[def-finite-discrete-memoryless-network-and-code]], or finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces with constant coordinates allowed. Encoders are measurable functions of a node's own message and its past outputs; a destination knows its own message. Choose a finite variable $Q$ and measurable kernels with joint law
$$P_Q\prod_k P_{X_k|Q}\,W(dy_{[N]}|x_{[N]})\prod_k P_{\hat Y_k|X_k,Y_k,Q}.$$
Assume AC in the Euclidean case. For each positive-probability $q$, require a measurable version of the local log likelihood
$$\iota_{k,q}=\log\frac{dP_{\hat Y_k|X_k,Y_k,q}}{dP_{\hat Y_k|X_k,q}}(\hat Y_k)$$
to exist and be square-integrable under the target law. For a destination $d$, nonempty $A\subseteq[N]\setminus\{d\}$, and $U\subseteq A^c\setminus\{d\}$, put $C_0=(A\cup U)^c$, let $P_{d,q}$ be the target marginal law of $(X_{[N]},\hat Y_{[N]},Y_d)$ given $q$, and define
$$Q_{d,A,U,q}=P_{X_{A^c},\hat Y_{C_0},Y_d|q}\prod_{k\in A}P_{X_k|q}\prod_{k\in A\cup U}P_{\hat Y_k|X_k,q}.$$
Require $P_{d,q}\ll Q_{d,A,U,q}$ with a measurable square-integrable log likelihood under $P_{d,q}$. Require all mutual informations in the following cut expression to be finite:
$$F_d(A)=I(X_A;Y_d,\hat Y_{A^c}|X_{A^c},Q)-I(Y_A;\hat Y_A|X_{[N]},Y_d,\hat Y_{A^c},Q).$$
These likelihood and finiteness hypotheses hold automatically for finite alphabets; zero-mass target atoms are omitted. At any chosen constrained node let $c_k\ge0$ be a measurable input cost. Require either $\mathbb E[c_k(X_k)^2]<\infty$ and $\mathbb E[c_k(X_k)]<\Gamma_k$, or a deterministic input whose cost is at most $\Gamma_k$. The latter case includes an identically zero input under a zero budget. Unconstrained nodes and constant coordinates are permitted.

Every nonnegative rate tuple satisfying
$$\sum_{k\in A\cap\mathcal S}r_k<F_d(A)$$
for every $d\in\mathcal D$ and nonempty $A$ with $d\notin A$ and $A\cap\mathcal S\ne\varnothing$ is achievable by deterministic measurable causal codes. Each constrained node can satisfy $\sum_{t=1}^m c_k(X_{k,t})\le m\Gamma_k$ on every realized transmitted input sequence of code length $m$, and hence also its expected average-cost constraint. The closure of the union of these regions over admissible laws is achievable. Constant reconstructions are permitted. The separate all-zero tuple is achievable whenever one can choose fixed inputs obeying any imposed costs, regardless of negative cut expressions.

Assume AC. Let $U,V,Y,S$ take values in standard-Borel spaces. Then
$$I((U,V);Y|S)=I(U;Y|S)+I(V;Y|U,S)$$
and also
$$I((U,V);Y|S)=I(V;Y|S)+I(U;Y|V,S),$$
where these are equalities of extended nonnegative quantities. In particular, if the conditional law of $Y$ given $(U,V,S)$ depends only on $(V,S)$, then
$$I(U;Y|S)\le I(V;Y|S).$$

derivations.claim: Initially choose $0<P_i'<P_i$ when $P_i>0$, and set $X_i=0$ when $P_i=0$. On positive-power nodes take independent $X_i\sim N(0,P_i')$. Use the stated reconstruction kernels. Remove constant coordinates when writing densities. The remaining joint coordinates $(X,Y,\hat Y_{\mathcal Q})$ are an invertible linear image of the independent nonconstant inputs, channel noises and quantization noises: recover inputs first, channel noises from $Y-GX$, and quantization noises from $\hat Y_{\mathcal Q}-Y_{\mathcal Q}$. They therefore have a strictly positive nonsingular Gaussian density. Its needed marginal and conditional densities are likewise Gaussian with positive conditional covariance, so all local and reference likelihood ratios in [F2] exist measurably. Every log ratio is a constant plus a quadratic polynomial in Gaussian variables.

These log ratios are square-integrable: a quadratic polynomial squared is a finite sum of monomials of degree at most four, and Gaussian fourth moments are finite. Explicitly for a scalar $N(0,v)$ density, integrating by parts twice gives $\mathbb E Z^4=3v^2$; Gaussian coordinates have those scalar marginal laws, and $\mathbb E(Z_i^2Z_j^2)\le(\mathbb E Z_i^4\,\mathbb E Z_j^4)^{1/2}$. The input cost $c_i(x)=x^2$ also has finite second moment $3(P_i')^2$ and mean $P_i'<P_i$. All the Gaussian cut mutual informations are finite, as differences of finite Gaussian conditional log-density expectations. Thus every Euclidean hypothesis of [F2] holds at the positive-power nodes with slack square costs; zero-power inputs are fixed zero coordinates satisfying their constraints pointwise and need no shell constraint.

Apply [F2] with constant time-sharing variable, converting $r_i=R_i\ln2$. It gives precisely the first displayed strict cut inequalities at variances $P_i'$, since constant reconstructions may be deleted from both mutual informations. Its codes are deterministic and measurable, and every positive-power input word has empirical square cost at most a threshold strictly below $P_i$. Hence the expected average-power constraints in [F1] hold for the chosen deterministic code, independently of messages and selected compression indices. Zero-power nodes always send zero.

Increase $P_i'$ to $P_i$ simultaneously at positive-power nodes. Each mutual information in these finitely many cuts is a continuous function of the variances: its Gaussian entropy formula is a log determinant of a positive-definite conditional noise covariance plus a positive-semidefinite signal covariance. One may derive the formula directly from the Gaussian density: for positive-definite $K$, integration of its log density gives $h(N(0,K))=\tfrac12\ln((2\pi e)^m\det K)$ because the expected quadratic form is $m$. Conditional noise covariance is positive definite even at the limiting input variances. Therefore any tuple satisfying all strict inequalities at $P_i$ satisfies them at $P_i'$ sufficiently close to $P_i$. Use the codes from step 3.1, already satisfying the original power constraints. This proves the full chosen-$\mathcal Q$ achievability assertion, including arbitrary zero-power nodes.

For the target Gaussian law, conditioned on all inputs the noises at nodes in $A$ are independent of $(Y_d,\hat Y_{A^c\cap\mathcal Q})$, since $d\notin A$ and channel and quantization noises are independent across nodes. Each active source-side test channel adds independent unit quantization noise to unit channel noise. Using the density entropy formula from step 4.1 gives $I(Y_{A\cap\mathcal Q};\hat Y_{A\cap\mathcal Q}|X_{[N]},Y_d,\hat Y_{A^c\cap\mathcal Q})=\frac{|A\cap\mathcal Q|}{2}\log_2 2=\frac{|A\cap\mathcal Q|}{2}.$ Constants contribute zero. This calculation holds for every destination outside $A$ and all choices of powers.

When $\mathcal Q=[N]$ and all powers equal $P$, condition on $X_{A^c}$. The quantized vector $\hat Y_{A^c}$ is a known translation of $G(A)X_A$ plus an independent Gaussian vector of covariance $2I$. Its entropy minus the entropy of that noise, divided by $\ln2$, gives $I(X_A;\hat Y_{A^c}|X_{A^c})=\frac12\log_2\det\left(I+\frac P2G(A)G(A)^T\right).$ By [F3], adding $Y_d$ can only increase this positive mutual-information term. Subtracting the penalty $|A|/2$ from step 5.1 proves the sufficient determinant inequality for every destination outside every admissible cut. Step 4.1 makes all tuples satisfying this finite family of strict sufficient inequalities achievable.

The closure of the strict regions follows from [F2], or by selecting successively longer reliable codes for rate tuples tending to the claimed boundary points. For the all-zero tuple give every source a singleton message set, transmit zero at all nodes, and return the unique messages at every destination; error and power are both zero. This argument applies even if a sufficient cut expression is negative.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a finite nonempty alphabet, let $P$ be a probability vector on $\mathcal A$ in the sense of [[def-qa-35-finite-probability-entropy-and-stochastic-matrices]], and let $n\ge1$. Write $\operatorname{supp}(P):=\{a\in\mathcal A:P(a)>0\}$. For $a^n=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in\mathcal A^n$, its empirical distribution is $\widehat P_{a^n}(a):=n^{-1}|\{t:a_t=a\}|$. For $\delta>0$, define the support-restricted strongly typical set by
$$T_\delta^{(n)}(P):=\{a^n\in\operatorname{supp}(P)^n:|\widehat P_{a^n}(a)-P(a)|\le\delta P(a)\text{ for every }a\text{ with }P(a)>0\}.$$
For a finite joint law $P_{XA}$ and a fixed $x^n$, write $T_\delta^{(n)}(P_{A|X}\mid x^n):=\{a^n:(x^n,a^n)\in T_\delta^{(n)}(P_{XA})\}$. This conditional set is empty if $x^n$ is outside the support of $P_X$. Zero-probability letters are excluded exactly, so no logarithm of zero occurs in likelihood calculations on these sets.

Let $p_{XYZ}$ be a joint probability vector on finite alphabets and write $p_Z(z)$ for its marginal. It is the law of finite coordinate random elements on the canonical finite probability space from [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]] and [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]. For each $z$ with $p_Z(z)>0$, the conditional law $p_{XY|z}$ and its marginals $p_{X|z},p_{Y|z}$ are probability vectors by [[lem-it-finite-marginals-and-conditionals-are-pmfs]]. Define conditional mutual information in nats by

$$I(X;Y|Z):=\sum_{z:p_Z(z)>0}p_Z(z)D(p_{XY|z}\|p_{X|z}\otimes p_{Y|z}),$$

using the finite KL convention of [[def-qa-35-finite-probability-entropy-and-stochastic-matrices]], where $(p_{X|z}\otimes p_{Y|z})(x,y):=p_{X|z}(x)p_{Y|z}(y)$. A positive conditional joint mass forces both conditional marginals to be positive, so each displayed KL term is finite. Zero-mass conditioning values contribute no term. The base-$b$ version replaces $\ln$ by $\log_b$ inside the conditional KL sums.

derivations.claim: Fix $(v^n,x^n)\in T_{\delta_{\rm in}}^{(n)}(P_{VX})$. For this concentration calculation, draw an auxiliary word under $Q_n:=P_{U|X,V}^{\otimes n}(\cdot|x^n,v^n)$, rather than under the codebook law $C_n:=P_{U|V}^{\otimes n}(\cdot|v^n)$. For each positive-mass triple $(v,x,u)$, its empirical frequency under $Q_n$ has mean $\widehat P_{v^nx^n}(v,x)P_{U|X,V}(u|x,v)$, which differs from $P(v,x,u)$ by at most $\delta_{\rm in}P(v,x,u)$. Its variance is at most $1/(4n)$ because its indicator summands are independent across positions. Chebyshev's inequality with deviation threshold $(\delta_{\rm out}-\delta_{\rm in})P(v,x,u)$ and a finite union bound show that all positive-mass triple frequencies meet the $\delta_{\rm out}$ conditions with probability tending to one uniformly over the fixed input pairs. Zero-mass input pairs are absent and zero conditional-probability outputs are never generated.

For a triple word in $T_{\delta_{\rm out}}^{(n)}(P_{VXU})$, the exact likelihood ratio is $$\ln\frac{P_{U|X,V}^{\otimes n}(u^n|x^n,v^n)}{P_{U|V}^{\otimes n}(u^n|v^n)}=n\sum_{v,x,u}\widehat P_{v^nx^nu^n}(v,x,u)\ln\frac{P(u|x,v)}{P(u|v)}.$$ Every logarithm on the positive target support is finite. At the target law this finite sum is $I_P(X;U|V)$ by [F2]; it is linear in the empirical probabilities. Choose $\delta_{\rm out}$ small enough that it is at most $I_P(X;U|V)+\eta/3$ on every target-typical triple. On the target-typical set $T$, $Q_n/C_n\le e^{n(I_P(X;U|V)+\eta/3)}$ and $Q_n\ll C_n$. Therefore $C_n(T)\ge e^{-n(I_P(X;U|V)+\eta/3)}Q_n(T)$; step 1.1 gives a one-word match probability at least $(1-o(1))e^{-n(I_P(X;U|V)+\eta/3)}$, uniformly over the fixed input pairs.

The codewords are conditionally independent given $v^n$. If $p_n(v^n,x^n)$ is their one-word match probability and $M_n=\lceil e^{nR}\rceil$, then the probability that no word matches is $(1-p_n)^{M_n}\le e^{-M_np_n}$. Since $R>I_P(X;U|V)+\eta$, step 2.1 gives $M_np_n\to\infty$ uniformly, so the no-match probability tends to zero. This proves the covering claim.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a finite nonempty alphabet, let $P$ be a probability vector on $\mathcal A$ in the sense of [[def-qa-35-finite-probability-entropy-and-stochastic-matrices]], and let $n\ge1$. Write $\operatorname{supp}(P):=\{a\in\mathcal A:P(a)>0\}$. For $a^n=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in\mathcal A^n$, its empirical distribution is $\widehat P_{a^n}(a):=n^{-1}|\{t:a_t=a\}|$. For $\delta>0$, define the support-restricted strongly typical set by
$$T_\delta^{(n)}(P):=\{a^n\in\operatorname{supp}(P)^n:|\widehat P_{a^n}(a)-P(a)|\le\delta P(a)\text{ for every }a\text{ with }P(a)>0\}.$$
For a finite joint law $P_{XA}$ and a fixed $x^n$, write $T_\delta^{(n)}(P_{A|X}\mid x^n):=\{a^n:(x^n,a^n)\in T_\delta^{(n)}(P_{XA})\}$. This conditional set is empty if $x^n$ is outside the support of $P_X$. Zero-probability letters are excluded exactly, so no logarithm of zero occurs in likelihood calculations on these sets.

Let $p_{XYZ}$ be a joint probability vector on finite alphabets and write $p_Z(z)$ for its marginal. It is the law of finite coordinate random elements on the canonical finite probability space from [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]] and [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]. For each $z$ with $p_Z(z)>0$, the conditional law $p_{XY|z}$ and its marginals $p_{X|z},p_{Y|z}$ are probability vectors by [[lem-it-finite-marginals-and-conditionals-are-pmfs]]. Define conditional mutual information in nats by

$$I(X;Y|Z):=\sum_{z:p_Z(z)>0}p_Z(z)D(p_{XY|z}\|p_{X|z}\otimes p_{Y|z}),$$

using the finite KL convention of [[def-qa-35-finite-probability-entropy-and-stochastic-matrices]], where $(p_{X|z}\otimes p_{Y|z})(x,y):=p_{X|z}(x)p_{Y|z}(y)$. A positive conditional joint mass forces both conditional marginals to be positive, so each displayed KL term is finite. Zero-mass conditioning values contribute no term. The base-$b$ version replaces $\ln$ by $\log_b$ inside the conditional KL sums.

derivations.claim: For any jointly typical supported candidate $u^n$, $$\ln\frac{P_{U|V}^{\otimes n}(u^n|v^n)}{P_{U|V,Z}^{\otimes n}(u^n|v^n,z^n)}=n\sum_{v,u,z}\widehat P_{v^nu^nz^n}(v,u,z)\ln\frac{P(u|v)}{P(u|v,z)}.$$ The logarithms are finite on the positive target support. At $P_{VUZ}$ the finite sum equals $-I_P(U;Z|V)$ by [F2], and it is linear in the empirical probabilities. Choose the typicality tolerance small enough that every jointly typical triple has this sum at most $-I_P(U;Z|V)+\eta$.

Sum the likelihood-ratio expression of step 1.1 over the jointly typical candidates. The target conditional law is a probability vector, so its mass on that set is at most one; the exponential likelihood ratio is at most $e^{-n(I_P(U;Z|V)-\eta)}$. This gives the claimed bound. Joint typicality excludes unsupported triples; on each supported target triple both conditional probabilities in the ratio are positive.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(E,\mathcal E)$ and $(F,\mathcal F)$ be measurable spaces and let $P$ be a probability measure on $(E\times F,\mathcal E\otimes\mathcal F)$. Its marginals are $P_E(A)=P(A\times F)$ and $P_F(B)=P(E\times B)$. The product probability $P_E\otimes P_F$ exists by the finite product-measure theorem. For the absolutely continuous branch $P\ll P_E\otimes P_F$, assume AC as required by [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]; the non-absolutely-continuous branch below remains $+\infty$. Define the **measure-theoretic mutual information** of the joint law $P$ by
$$I(P):=D(P\|P_E\otimes P_F)\in[0,+\infty].$$
For random elements $X,Y$ with joint law $P_{XY}$, write $I(X;Y):=I(P_{XY})$. The logarithm convention is the natural logarithm, so finite values are in nats as fixed by [[def-it-information-units-and-logarithm-base]]. The divergence is directional in its two law arguments and is $+\infty$ when $P_{XY}\not\ll P_X\otimes P_Y$.

This definition uses only the joint law, not a choice of density or a difference of entropy quantities.

If $X$ has Lebesgue density $f$ on $\mathbb R^d$ and $\int f\ln f$ is a finite real number, its differential entropy in nats is $h(X):=-\int_{\mathbb R^d}f(x)\ln f(x)\,dx$. If $(X,S)$ has conditional densities $f_{X|S=s}$ for almost every $s$ and the indicated integral is finite, set $h(X|S):=\int h(f_{X|S=s})\,dP_S(s)$. We use only these finite-integral cases; differential entropy is not defined here by a formal subtraction of possibly infinite quantities.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. If a random vector $X\in\mathbb R^d$ has a Lebesgue density, finite mean $m$, positive-definite covariance $K$, and finite differential entropy $h(X)=-\int f\ln f$, then
$$h(X)\le \frac12\ln\bigl((2\pi e)^d\det K\bigr).$$
Equality holds exactly when $X$ has the Gaussian law $N_d(m,K)$.

Assume AC. Let $Z\in\mathbb C$ have a Lebesgue density, finite mean $\mu$, finite differential entropy, and positive-definite real covariance matrix $K$ for $(\operatorname{Re}Z,\operatorname{Im}Z)$. Put $\sigma^2=\mathbb E|Z-\mu|^2=\operatorname{tr}K$. Then
$$h(Z)\le\ln(\pi e\sigma^2).$$
Equality holds exactly for the circular complex Gaussian law $\mathcal{CN}(\mu,\sigma^2)$ with density $(\pi\sigma^2)^{-1}\exp(-|z-\mu|^2/\sigma^2)$.

Let $f$ be a Lebesgue probability density on $\mathbb R^d$ with $\|f\|_\infty<\infty$ and $\int |x|^2f(x)\,dx<\infty$. Then $\int f(x)|\ln f(x)|\,dx<\infty$, so the differential entropy in [[def-it-real-differential-entropy]] is a finite real number.

derivations.claim: The output density is the convolution $f_Y(y)=\int g_Z(y-ax)P_X(dx)$, so $0<f_Y\le\|g_Z\|_\infty<\infty$, and $Y$ has finite second moment. By [F5], $\int f_Y|\ln f_Y|<\infty$, so [F2] defines a finite differential entropy $h(Y)$.

The positive Gaussian noise density makes $f_Y(y)>0$. Relative to $P_X(dx)f_Y(y)dy$, the joint law of $(X,Y)$ has density $g_Z(y-ax)/f_Y(y)$. By [F1], $$I(X;Y)=\int P_X(dx)\int g_Z(y-ax)\ln\frac{g_Z(y-ax)}{f_Y(y)}dy=h(Y)-h(Z).$$ The two logarithmic integrals are finite by step 1.1 and the Gaussian density formula, so this identity involves no subtraction of infinite quantities.

Independence gives $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=1+|a|^2v$. Apply [F3] and the real Gaussian noise entropy in the real case, or [F4] and $h(Z)=\ln(\pi e)$ in the complex case. Step 2.1 then yields $I(X;Y)\le\kappa\ln(1+|a|^2v)$ nats. Since $v\le\mathbb E|X|^2$, division by $\ln2$ gives the corresponding bit bound. For the stated Gaussian inputs, the output is Gaussian of the same real or circular complex type and attains the matching maximum-entropy equality.

The two-user Gaussian interference channel has independent messages, separate encoders, and outputs
$$Y_1=h_{11}X_1+h_{21}X_2+Z_1,\qquad Y_2=h_{12}X_1+h_{22}X_2+Z_2.$$
For the **real model**, $X_i,h_{ji},Z_j$ are real and $Z_j\sim N(0,1)$. For the **complex model**, the inputs and gains are complex and $Z_j\sim\mathcal{CN}(0,1)$ with density $\pi^{-1}e^{-|z|^2}$. The receiver-noise variables are independent across receivers and channel uses and independent of the messages, so the channel is memoryless. Each power budget satisfies $P_i\ge0$. A length-$n$ code has independent uniform messages $M_i$ on $[m_i]$ for integers $m_i\ge1$, deterministic separate encoders $X_i^n=f_i(M_i)$, and decoders $\widehat M_i=g_i(Y_i^n)$; no feedback is present. The expected average-power constraints are $n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^n\mathbb E[X_{i,t}^2]\le P_i$ in the real model and $n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^n\mathbb E|X_{i,t}|^2\le P_i$ in the complex model, with expectations under the uniform message law. The average joint error is $\Pr\{(\widehat M_1,\widehat M_2)\ne(M_1,M_2)\}$. For either model define
$$\mathrm{SNR}_1=|h_{11}|^2P_1,\quad \mathrm{SNR}_2=|h_{22}|^2P_2,\quad \mathrm{INR}_1=|h_{21}|^2P_2,\quad \mathrm{INR}_2=|h_{12}|^2P_1.$$
Rates are bits per use, $R_i=n^{-1}\log_2m_i$. For a scalar unit-noise AWGN link $Y=aX+Z$ with power constraint $P$, the capacity is $\kappa\log_2(1+|a|^2P)$, attained by a centered real Gaussian input or a circular complex Gaussian input; $\kappa=1/2$ in the real model and $\kappa=1$ in the complex model.

Let $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ be IID square-integrable real random variables, with $\mu=\mathbb EX_1$ and $\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(X_1)$. For $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nX_k$,
$$\mathbb E|S_n/n-\mu|^2=\sigma^2/n,$$
and $S_n/n\to\mu$ in $L^2$ and in probability. Also $\mathbb P(|S_n/n-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)\le\sigma^2/(n\varepsilon^2)$ for $\varepsilon>0$.

Assume AC. Let $X$ be real or complex with finite second moment, let $Z$ be independent unit-variance Gaussian noise, and let $Y=aX+Z$. In the real case take $Z\sim N(0,1)$ and $a\in\mathbb R$; in the complex case take $Z\sim\mathcal{CN}(0,1)$ with density $\pi^{-1}e^{-|z|^2}$ and $a\in\mathbb C$. Put $v=\mathbb E|X-\mathbb EX|^2$ and $\kappa=1/2$ in the real case, $\kappa=1$ in the complex case. Then
$$I(X;Y)\le\kappa\ln(1+|a|^2v)\le\kappa\ln(1+|a|^2\mathbb E|X|^2)$$
in nats; division by $\ln2$ gives the corresponding bit formula.
Equality in the first inequality holds when $X$ is Gaussian in the real case or circular complex Gaussian in the complex case, including the zero-variance case.

derivations.claim: Generate independent message-indexed Gaussian codebooks for $U_1,V_1,U_2,V_2$, with each coordinate law matching its assigned power. The two components at transmitter $i$ sum to a Gaussian input of power $P_i$; when one component has zero power, set its rate to zero and omit it. The private component of user 2 contributes independent Gaussian noise at receiver 1, and the private component of user 1 contributes independent Gaussian noise at receiver 2, with the variances $N_1,N_2$ stated above.

At receiver $j$, let $\mathcal D_j$ be its three decoded streams. For every nonempty $T\subseteq\mathcal D_j$, define the information density $\imath_{j,T}(u_T;y|u_{T^c})=\ln\frac{w_j(y|u_{\mathcal D_j})}{\int w_j(y|u_T',u_{T^c})\prod_{s\in T}P_{U_s}(du_s')},$ where $w_j$ is the Gaussian output density with the other user's private stream included in its noise variance $N_j$. Decode the positive-rate streams by threshold tests for every subset with positive total rate. A zero-rate stream has a singleton message set, so it creates no competing codeword. Choose thresholds between $\ln2$ times each subset rate and its mutual information in nats. For each tested true subset, the information density is a sum of IID quadratic functions of Gaussian variables with finite variance, so [F2] makes the tests pass with probability tending to one. Condition on the complementary decoded streams and rescale the output by $N_j^{-1/2}$; [F3] and its Gaussian equality case give the stated subset mutual information in nats.

For either receiver and any nonempty subset $T$ of incorrectly decoded streams, $T$ has positive total rate; its false codewords are independent of the output and the correctly decoded streams. The likelihood ratio for that subset has mean one under this false-candidate law, so Markov's inequality bounds the chance of passing a threshold $n\tau_T$ by $e^{-n\tau_T}$. There are at most $e^{n\ln2\sum_{s\in T}R_s+o(n)}$ false tuples. The union bound over the tested subsets tends to zero because each threshold exceeds the corresponding rate sum in nats.

The ensemble error argument alone does not yet impose deterministic codebook powers. For fixed $0<\varepsilon<1$, instead generate each positive component at power $(1-\varepsilon)P_s$. The finitely many strict positive-rate subset inequalities remain valid for sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, by continuity; zero-power components have zero rate and are omitted. For user $i$, let $B_{i,j}$ be the coordinate-$j$ input energy $|U_i+V_i|^2$, averaged over all of its common/private message indices, including the cross term. These variables are IID across coordinates, have mean $(1-\varepsilon)P_i$, and satisfy $\mathbb E B_{i,j}^2\le\mathbb E|U_i+V_i|^4\le3P_i^2$ by Jensen and the real Gaussian fourth moment; in the circular complex case the sharper constant is $2P_i^2$. Thus the codebook's expected average input power has variance at most $3P_i^2/n$. Chebyshev shows that the probability of either user's power exceeding its unscaled constraint tends to zero, while Markov applied to the ensemble sum of receiver errors shows that the probability of an error exceeding the square root of that ensemble mean tends to zero. Consequently some deterministic codebook simultaneously meets both power constraints and has vanishing receiver errors. If $P_i=0$, its codeword is identically zero and no concentration is needed. Taking achievable closures and then $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ recovers the stated component powers and all boundary split rates by continuity. Singleton streams create no competing codewords; if every rate is zero, use the all-zero code and obtain zero error. This proves the full real and complex fixed-split region without changing the statement.

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ be IID square-integrable real random variables, with $\mu=\mathbb EX_1$ and $\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(X_1)$. For $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nX_k$,
$$\mathbb E|S_n/n-\mu|^2=\sigma^2/n,$$
and $S_n/n\to\mu$ in $L^2$ and in probability. Also $\mathbb P(|S_n/n-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)\le\sigma^2/(n\varepsilon^2)$ for $\varepsilon>0$.

Assume AC. Let $X$ be real or complex with finite second moment, let $Z$ be independent unit-variance Gaussian noise, and let $Y=aX+Z$. In the real case take $Z\sim N(0,1)$ and $a\in\mathbb R$; in the complex case take $Z\sim\mathcal{CN}(0,1)$ with density $\pi^{-1}e^{-|z|^2}$ and $a\in\mathbb C$. Put $v=\mathbb E|X-\mathbb EX|^2$ and $\kappa=1/2$ in the real case, $\kappa=1$ in the complex case. Then
$$I(X;Y)\le\kappa\ln(1+|a|^2v)\le\kappa\ln(1+|a|^2\mathbb E|X|^2)$$
in nats; division by $\ln2$ gives the corresponding bit formula.
Equality in the first inequality holds when $X$ is Gaussian in the real case or circular complex Gaussian in the complex case, including the zero-variance case.

derivations.claim: Use the stated full powers $P_i$ in the codebook laws and information densities. Generate $M_i=\lceil2^{nR_i}\rceil$ codewords independently for each sender, with IID coordinates from its specified centered real or circular complex Gaussian input law. For a nonempty subset $S\subseteq\{1,2\}$, define its one-use information density by $$\imath_S(x_1,x_2;y):=\ln\frac{w(y|x_1,x_2)}{p_{Y|X_{S^c}}(y|x_{S^c})},$$ where $w$ is the Gaussian channel output density and the denominator averages $w$ over the Gaussian input laws of the senders in $S$. Use the sum of these densities over coordinates as the threshold statistic. For each $S$ with $R(S):=\sum_{i\in S}R_i>0$, choose $\tau_S$ so that $R(S)\ln2<\tau_S<I_S$, where $I_S=\mathbb E\imath_S$ is in nats. A subset with $R(S)=0$ has no false-message candidates and needs no threshold. For each tested subset the true statistic is a sum of IID quadratic polynomials in Gaussian variables with finite variance; [F2] makes its threshold test pass with probability tending to one.

If a nonempty subset $S$ of positive total rate is wrong, its independently generated candidate codewords are independent of the output conditional on the correct codewords in $S^c$. By the definition in step 1.1, the exponential of the threshold statistic is the likelihood ratio of the true conditional output density to the density averaged over the candidate input law; its expectation under the false-candidate law is one. The nonnegative likelihood ratio and Markov's inequality therefore bound acceptance by $e^{-n\tau_S}$. Subsets of zero total rate cannot be wrong because all their message sets are singletons.

For each tested subset $S$, the number of false candidates is at most $e^{nR(S)\ln2+o(n)}$, so the union bound gives ensemble-average error $e_n\to0$. For $P_i>0$, write $K_i=nM_i$ and $D_i=\sum_{t,m}(|X_{i,t}(m)|^2-P_i)$; the power constraint is $D_i\le0$. Gaussian moments and independence give $\mathbb E D_i=0$, $v_i:=\mathbb E D_i^2>0$, and $\mathbb E D_i^4\le15v_i^2$: in the real case the ratio is $3+12/K_i$, and in the complex case it is $3+6/K_i$. Hölder gives $v_i\le(\mathbb E|D_i|)^{2/3}(\mathbb E D_i^4)^{1/3}$, hence $\mathbb E|D_i|\ge\sqrt{v_i/15}$. Since $\mathbb E(D_i)_-=\mathbb E|D_i|/2$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\Pr\{D_i<0\}\ge1/60$. If $P_i=0$, its codebook is identically zero. The two independently generated codebooks therefore meet both power constraints with probability at least $1/3600$. Markov bounds the probability of error exceeding $\sqrt{e_n}$ by $\sqrt{e_n}$; for large $n$ this is less than $1/3600$, so there exists a deterministic power-feasible codebook with error at most $\sqrt{e_n}\to0$ (if $e_n=0$, error is zero almost surely). For any fixed finite list of receivers satisfying their subset inequalities, apply steps 1.1–2.1 at each receiver to this same input ensemble and replace $e_n$ by the sum of their average errors; the identical selection then makes every receiver's error vanish.

For each nonempty subset $S$, condition on the other codewords. The remaining signal is a centered real or circular complex Gaussian with variance $\sum_{i\in S}|a_i|^2P_i$. Its mutual information with the unit-noise output is exactly $I_S=\kappa\ln(1+\sum_{i\in S}|a_i|^2P_i)$ nats by [F3] and its Gaussian equality case. Dividing by $\ln2$ gives the rates in bits. Step 3.1 selects deterministic codes from exactly the full-variance ensemble stated above, establishing the strict region under the allowed powers. If both rates are zero, singleton message sets achieve zero error. Taking closure gives the stated closed MAC region, including faces where a zero-rate subset has zero mutual information.

A **finite discrete memoryless relay channel** is the three-node instance of [[def-finite-discrete-memoryless-network-and-code]] with source input $X\in\mathcal X$, relay input $X_r\in\mathcal X_r$, relay observation $Y_r\in\mathcal Y_r$, destination observation $Y\in\mathcal Y$, and transition law $W(y_r,y\mid x,x_r)$. For a positive integer message-set size $M$, the one-way message is uniform on $[M]$ and the destination estimates it from $Y^n$.

In the **relay-only causal model**, $X_i=f_i(M)$ and $X_{r,i}=g_i(Y_r^{i-1})$. In the **full output-feedback model**, both encoders know the past pair $(Y^{i-1},Y_r^{i-1})$, so $X_i=f_i(M,Y^{i-1},Y_r^{i-1})$ and $X_{r,i}=g_i(Y^{i-1},Y_r^{i-1})$. In either model the channel outputs at time $i$ are drawn from $W(\cdot,\cdot\mid X_i,X_{r,i})$; no encoder sees a current-time output before choosing its current input. The rate is $n^{-1}\ln M$, and achievability uses average error under the uniform message law.

Let $P$ be a probability vector on a finite alphabet $\mathcal A$. For every $\delta>0$, the support-restricted strongly typical set $T_\delta^{(n)}(P)$ of [[def-it-finite-strongly-typical-set]] satisfies
$$P^{\otimes n}(T_\delta^{(n)}(P))\longrightarrow1\qquad(n\to\infty).$$

Let $(V,U,Z)$ have any joint law $P_{VUZ}$ on finite alphabets. Fix $\eta>0$. For every sufficiently small strong-typicality tolerance, every sufficiently large $n$, and every fixed $(v^n,z^n)$ typical for the marginal $P_{VZ}$, an independent candidate word drawn from the product law $P_{U|V}^{\otimes n}(\cdot|v^n)$ satisfies
$$\Pr\{(v^n,U^n,z^n)\text{ is jointly typical for }P_{VUZ}\}\le e^{-n(I_P(U;Z|V)-\eta)}.$$
The conclusion includes the case that $V$ is constant, giving the exponent $I_P(U;Z)$.

derivations.claim: Choose $\epsilon>0$ so that $R+\epsilon$ is below both mutual informations. For every block $b\in\{1,\ldots,B+1\}$, independently generate a relay codebook $x_{r,b}^n(w)$ with $w\in[\lceil e^{nR}\rceil]$, each word IID from $P_{X_r}$. Given each relay word, generate source words $x_b^n(m,w)$ independently according to $\prod_iP_{X|X_r}(x_i|x_{r,b,i})$. Set $w_0=w_{B+1}=1$ as fixed dummy indices and use $w_1,\ldots,w_B$ for the $B$ messages. In block $b$, the source sends $x_b^n(w_b,w_{b-1})$ and the relay sends $x_{r,b}^n(w_{b-1})$. This is causal under [F1].

At the end of block $b$, the relay tests candidate $w_b$ using $(x_{r,b}^n(w_{b-1}),x_b^n(w_b,w_{b-1}),y_r^n(b))$ and accepts the unique jointly typical candidate. The true triple has the IID law $P_{X_r}P_{X|X_r}W_{Y_r|X,X_r}$, so [F2] makes its test pass with probability tending to one. For a wrong candidate, its source word is conditionally independent of the relay observation given the known relay word; [F3] bounds a false test by $e^{-n(I(X;Y_r|X_r)-\epsilon)}$. There are at most $e^{nR}$ false indices, so the union bound tends to zero because $R+\epsilon<I(X;Y_r|X_r)$.

The destination decodes backward over blocks $b=B+1,B,\ldots,2$. It knows $w_b$ from the next block (or as the fixed dummy $w_{B+1}$), and tests each candidate $w_{b-1}$ against the block-$b$ source and relay codewords and $y^n(b)$. The true tuple is IID with law $P_{X_r}P_{X|X_r}W_Y$ and passes by [F2]. For a wrong candidate, the pair of candidate codewords is independent of the output generated by the true pair; [F3] bounds a false test by $e^{-n(I(X,X_r;Y)-\epsilon)}$. The union bound over at most $e^{nR}$ wrong indices tends to zero because $R+\epsilon<I(X,X_r;Y)$.

For positive $R$ there are $B$ message blocks and $B+1$ channel blocks, so the rate tends to $BR/(B+1)$ as $n\to\infty$. For fixed $B$, the ensemble-average error tends to zero by steps 2.1, 2.2; then letting $B\to\infty$ approaches $R$. The strict slack permits the typicality tolerances to shrink with $n$, and closure gives the positive-rate part.

At $R=0$, use a singleton message set and let the destination always return its sole element; the error probability is zero for every blocklength. Thus the zero-rate case is included even if one of the mutual informations vanishes.

Let $p_{XYZ}$ be a joint probability vector on finite alphabets and write $p_Z(z)$ for its marginal. It is the law of finite coordinate random elements on the canonical finite probability space from [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]] and [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]. For each $z$ with $p_Z(z)>0$, the conditional law $p_{XY|z}$ and its marginals $p_{X|z},p_{Y|z}$ are probability vectors by [[lem-it-finite-marginals-and-conditionals-are-pmfs]]. Define conditional mutual information in nats by

$$I(X;Y|Z):=\sum_{z:p_Z(z)>0}p_Z(z)D(p_{XY|z}\|p_{X|z}\otimes p_{Y|z}),$$

using the finite KL convention of [[def-qa-35-finite-probability-entropy-and-stochastic-matrices]], where $(p_{X|z}\otimes p_{Y|z})(x,y):=p_{X|z}(x)p_{Y|z}(y)$. A positive conditional joint mass forces both conditional marginals to be positive, so each displayed KL term is finite. Zero-mass conditioning values contribute no term. The base-$b$ version replaces $\ln$ by $\log_b$ inside the conditional KL sums.

For finite $X,Y,Z$ with a joint pmf,

$$H(X,Y|Z)=H(X|Z)+H(Y|X,Z),$$

and

$$I(X;Y,Z)=I(X;Z)+I(X;Y|Z).$$

In particular, $I(X;Y)=H(X)-H(X|Y)=H(Y)-H(Y|X)$. All terms are finite.

For finite $X,Y,Z$,

$$I(X;Y|Z)=H(X|Z)+H(Y|Z)-H(X,Y|Z)\ge0.$$

Equality holds if and only if, for every $z$ with $p_Z(z)>0$, the conditional joint pmf factors as $p_{XY|z}=p_{X|z}p_{Y|z}$; this is conditional independence given $Z$.

Expanding in the other order gives $$I(X,Q;Y\mid Z)=I(Q;Y\mid Z)+I(X;Y\mid Z,Q).$$ The first term on the right is nonnegative by [F3], proving the inequality.

For finite random sequences $X^n=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ and $Y^n=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n)$, define the **directed information** from $X^n$ to $Y^n$ by
$$I(X^n\to Y^n):=\sum_{i=1}^n I(X^i;Y_i\mid Y^{i-1}),$$
where $X^i=(X_1,\ldots,X_i)$ and $Y^0$ is the empty tuple. For a third finite sequence $Z^n$, define the causally conditioned version
$$I(X^n\to Y^n\Vert Z^n):=\sum_{i=1}^n I(X^i;Y_i\mid Y^{i-1},Z^i).$$
All conditional mutual information terms use the finite nats convention of [[def-it-finite-conditional-mutual-information]]. The conditioning includes $Z_i$ because it is the current side-information symbol available at the receiving end of the directed-information term; $Y^{i-1}$ and $Z^{i-1}$ are the past.

For finite $X,Y,Z$ with a joint pmf,

$$H(X,Y|Z)=H(X|Z)+H(Y|X,Z),$$

and

$$I(X;Y,Z)=I(X;Z)+I(X;Y|Z).$$

In particular, $I(X;Y)=H(X)-H(X|Y)=H(Y)-H(Y|X)$. All terms are finite.

derivations.claim: Expand $I(X^n;Y^n)$ by the chain rule in the order $Y_1,\ldots,Y_n$ to obtain $\sum_{i=1}^n I(X^n;Y_i\mid Y^{i-1})$. For each $i$, split $X^n=(X^i,X_{i+1}^n)$ and apply the chain rule again: $$I(X^n;Y_i\mid Y^{i-1})=I(X^i;Y_i\mid Y^{i-1})+I(X_{i+1}^n;Y_i\mid X^i,Y^{i-1}).$$ Summing the first terms gives $I(X^n\to Y^n)$ by [F1].

Write $I(X^n;Y^n)=H(X^n)-H(X^n\mid Y^n)$ and each term of $I(X^n\to Y^n)$ as $H(Y_i\mid Y^{i-1})-H(Y_i\mid Y^{i-1},X^i)$. The interleaved chain rule gives $$H(X^n\mid Y^n)+H(Y^n)=H(X^n,Y^n)=\sum_i\bigl[H(X_i\mid X^{i-1},Y^{i-1})+H(Y_i\mid Y^{i-1},X^i)\bigr].$$ Subtracting the directed-information terms therefore yields $$I(X^n;Y^n)-I(X^n\to Y^n)=H(X^n)-\sum_{i=1}^n H(X_i\mid X^{i-1},Y^{i-1}).$$ The finite chain rule expands $H(X^n)=\sum_i H(X_i\mid X^{i-1})$, so the right-hand side is $\sum_i I(X_i;Y^{i-1}\mid X^{i-1})=\sum_i I(Y^{i-1};X_i\mid X^{i-1})$ by symmetry of finite mutual information. This is the stated feedback term, including its zero $i=1$ summand.

A **finite two-user interference channel** is the two-sender, two-receiver memoryless channel with finite nonempty input alphabets $\mathcal X_1,\mathcal X_2$, finite nonempty output alphabets $\mathcal Y_1,\mathcal Y_2$, and transition law $W(y_1,y_2|x_1,x_2)$. Independent uniform messages $M_1,M_2$ on finite nonempty sets are encoded separately as $X_1^n=f_1(M_1)$ and $X_2^n=f_2(M_2)$; receiver $i$ estimates $M_i$ from $Y_i^n$. The **strong-interference regime** means that, for every product law $P_{X_1}P_{X_2}$,
$$I(X_1;Y_1|X_2)\le I(X_1;Y_2|X_2),\qquad I(X_2;Y_2|X_1)\le I(X_2;Y_1|X_1).$$
The inequalities are evaluated under the stated product law and the channel. They are universal hypotheses over input laws, not just inequalities at a chosen optimizing distribution.

For finite $X,Y,Z$,

$$I(X;Y|Z)=H(X|Z)+H(Y|Z)-H(X,Y|Z)\ge0.$$

Equality holds if and only if, for every $z$ with $p_Z(z)>0$, the conditional joint pmf factors as $p_{XY|z}=p_{X|z}p_{Y|z}$; this is conditional independence given $Z$.

For finite $X,Y,Z$ with a joint pmf,

$$H(X,Y|Z)=H(X|Z)+H(Y|X,Z),$$

and

$$I(X;Y,Z)=I(X;Z)+I(X;Y|Z).$$

In particular, $I(X;Y)=H(X)-H(X|Y)=H(Y)-H(Y|X)$. All terms are finite.

derivations.claim: First fix $x_2^n$. Under this conditioning, $Y_1^n$ and $Y_2^n$ are product channels from $X_1^n$, with the $i$th channel determined by $x_{2,i}$. Set $A^n=Y_2^n$, $B^n=Y_1^n$, and $J_i=I(X_1^n;A^i,B_{i+1}^n\mid X_2^n=x_2^n)$ for $i=0,\ldots,n$. The chain rule [F3] gives $$J_i-J_{i-1}=I(X_1^n;A_i\mid A^{i-1},B_{i+1}^n,x_2^n)-I(X_1^n;B_i\mid A^{i-1},B_{i+1}^n,x_2^n).$$ Because the channel is memoryless across coordinates, each term reduces to the mutual information between $X_{1,i}$ and that coordinate's output conditional on the common context $(A^{i-1},B_{i+1}^n,x_2^n)$. For each value of this context, [F1] applies to the induced law of $X_{1,i}$ and fixed $x_{2,i}$, so $J_i-J_{i-1}\ge0$. Summing over $i$ yields $I(X_1^n;Y_2^n|X_2^n=x_2^n)\ge I(X_1^n;Y_1^n|X_2^n=x_2^n)$. Average over $X_2^n$.

Exchange the user indices and exchange $Y_1,Y_2$. The second strong-interference inequality in [F1] gives the same telescoping argument with receiver 1 as the more informative output for user 2. Averaging over $X_1^n$ gives $I(X_2^n;Y_1^n|X_1^n)\ge I(X_2^n;Y_2^n|X_1^n)$.

A **finite discrete memoryless network (DMN)** has a node set $[N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ for an integer $N\ge1$, finite nonempty input alphabets $\mathcal X_k$ and output alphabets $\mathcal Y_k$, and one transition probability vector $W(y_1,\ldots,y_N\mid x_1,\ldots,x_N)$ for each input tuple. At each use, conditional on the current input tuple, the output tuple is drawn from this vector independently of earlier uses.

Node $k$ may have an independent uniform message $M_k$ in a finite nonempty set $\mathcal M_k$ and a destination set $D_k\subseteq[N]$. A length-$n$ **causal code** consists of encoders $X_{k,i}=f_{k,i}(M_k,Y_k^{i-1})$ and, for each destination $d\in D_k$, a decoder $\widehat M_{kd}=g_{kd}(Y_d^n,M_d)$; here $Y_k^{i-1}=(Y_{k,1},\ldots,Y_{k,i-1})$, with the empty tuple at $i=1$. The average error is the probability that any required estimate differs from its message. A rate tuple is achievable if a sequence of such codes has error tending to zero and message-set rates tending to at least that tuple; the capacity region is the closure of achievable tuples.

All logarithms, mutual informations and rates in this lemma are in nats. Consider a memoryless network with finite node set $[N]$, source set $\mathcal S$, destination set $\mathcal D$, and independent uniform source messages, each required by every destination. Alphabets are either all finite, as in [[def-finite-discrete-memoryless-network-and-code]], or finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces with constant coordinates allowed. Encoders are measurable functions of a node's own message and its past outputs; a destination knows its own message. Choose a finite variable $Q$ and measurable kernels with joint law
$$P_Q\prod_k P_{X_k|Q}\,W(dy_{[N]}|x_{[N]})\prod_k P_{\hat Y_k|X_k,Y_k,Q}.$$
Assume AC in the Euclidean case. For each positive-probability $q$, require a measurable version of the local log likelihood
$$\iota_{k,q}=\log\frac{dP_{\hat Y_k|X_k,Y_k,q}}{dP_{\hat Y_k|X_k,q}}(\hat Y_k)$$
to exist and be square-integrable under the target law. For a destination $d$, nonempty $A\subseteq[N]\setminus\{d\}$, and $U\subseteq A^c\setminus\{d\}$, put $C_0=(A\cup U)^c$, let $P_{d,q}$ be the target marginal law of $(X_{[N]},\hat Y_{[N]},Y_d)$ given $q$, and define
$$Q_{d,A,U,q}=P_{X_{A^c},\hat Y_{C_0},Y_d|q}\prod_{k\in A}P_{X_k|q}\prod_{k\in A\cup U}P_{\hat Y_k|X_k,q}.$$
Require $P_{d,q}\ll Q_{d,A,U,q}$ with a measurable square-integrable log likelihood under $P_{d,q}$. Require all mutual informations in the following cut expression to be finite:
$$F_d(A)=I(X_A;Y_d,\hat Y_{A^c}|X_{A^c},Q)-I(Y_A;\hat Y_A|X_{[N]},Y_d,\hat Y_{A^c},Q).$$
These likelihood and finiteness hypotheses hold automatically for finite alphabets; zero-mass target atoms are omitted. At any chosen constrained node let $c_k\ge0$ be a measurable input cost. Require either $\mathbb E[c_k(X_k)^2]<\infty$ and $\mathbb E[c_k(X_k)]<\Gamma_k$, or a deterministic input whose cost is at most $\Gamma_k$. The latter case includes an identically zero input under a zero budget. Unconstrained nodes and constant coordinates are permitted.

Every nonnegative rate tuple satisfying
$$\sum_{k\in A\cap\mathcal S}r_k<F_d(A)$$
for every $d\in\mathcal D$ and nonempty $A$ with $d\notin A$ and $A\cap\mathcal S\ne\varnothing$ is achievable by deterministic measurable causal codes. Each constrained node can satisfy $\sum_{t=1}^m c_k(X_{k,t})\le m\Gamma_k$ on every realized transmitted input sequence of code length $m$, and hence also its expected average-cost constraint. The closure of the union of these regions over admissible laws is achievable. Constant reconstructions are permitted. The separate all-zero tuple is achievable whenever one can choose fixed inputs obeying any imposed costs, regardless of negative cut expressions.

Let $p_{XYZ}$ be a joint probability vector on finite alphabets and write $p_Z(z)$ for its marginal. It is the law of finite coordinate random elements on the canonical finite probability space from [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]] and [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]. For each $z$ with $p_Z(z)>0$, the conditional law $p_{XY|z}$ and its marginals $p_{X|z},p_{Y|z}$ are probability vectors by [[lem-it-finite-marginals-and-conditionals-are-pmfs]]. Define conditional mutual information in nats by

$$I(X;Y|Z):=\sum_{z:p_Z(z)>0}p_Z(z)D(p_{XY|z}\|p_{X|z}\otimes p_{Y|z}),$$

using the finite KL convention of [[def-qa-35-finite-probability-entropy-and-stochastic-matrices]], where $(p_{X|z}\otimes p_{Y|z})(x,y):=p_{X|z}(x)p_{Y|z}(y)$. A positive conditional joint mass forces both conditional marginals to be positive, so each displayed KL term is finite. Zero-mass conditioning values contribute no term. The base-$b$ version replaces $\ln$ by $\log_b$ inside the conditional KL sums.

derivations.claim: For each positive-probability value of $Q$, use the target law in the statement. Its alphabets are finite. A target-positive joint atom has positive local marginal-reconstruction probability and positive reference probability for every reference law in [F2], because all its displayed marginal factors are positive. Thus every required likelihood ratio is finite on target support; the finitely many log values are bounded and hence square-integrable. All cut informations are finite. No cost constraint is imposed. These observations verify every hypothesis of the finite branch of [F2], including arbitrary zero-probability letters, which can simply be omitted.

Apply [F2] with this law and source/destination sets. Its independent messages, causal encoders and destination side information have exactly the conventions of [F1]. Its cut expression is $I(X_A;Y_d,\hat Y_{A^c}|X_{A^c},Q)-I(Y_A;\hat Y_A|X_{[N]},Y_d,\hat Y_{A^c},Q)$ for every required $A,d$, so every tuple satisfying the displayed strict inequalities is achievable. A constant reconstruction is allowed in [F2] and contributes zero local and conditional information.

The closure-of-union conclusion follows from [F2], or by choosing a sequence of strict-region laws and rate tuples tending to the claimed point and selecting successively longer codes with error tending to zero and rates tending to that point. Independently, singleton message sets at every source and a destination that returns those unique messages have error exactly zero; this realizes the separate zero tuple even when a cut expression is negative.

Consider a finite DMN as in [[def-finite-discrete-memoryless-network-and-code]]. Let $\mathcal S$ be a source-node set, let $\mathcal D$ be a destination-node set, and let each source $k\in\mathcal S$ send an independent message of rate $R_k$ to every destination. For a finite time-sharing variable $Q$, choose
$$P_Q\prod_{k=1}^N P_{X_k|Q}\prod_{k=1}^N P_{\hat Y_k|Y_k,X_k,Q}.$$
For every destination $d\in\mathcal D$ and every nonempty cut set $A\subseteq[N]$ with $A\cap\mathcal S\ne\varnothing$ and $d\notin A$, the noisy-network-coding inner bound is
$$\sum_{k\in A\cap\mathcal S}R_k < I(X_A;Y_d,\hat Y_{A^c}\mid X_{A^c},Q)-I(Y_A;\hat Y_A\mid X_{[N]},Y_d,\hat Y_{A^c},Q).$$
The closure of the union of these rate tuples, together with the all-zero rate tuple, is achievable; the separate zero tuple is attained by singleton message sets even if some cut expression is negative. A constant reconstruction $\hat Y_k$ is permitted at any node.

A **finite discrete memoryless relay channel** is the three-node instance of [[def-finite-discrete-memoryless-network-and-code]] with source input $X\in\mathcal X$, relay input $X_r\in\mathcal X_r$, relay observation $Y_r\in\mathcal Y_r$, destination observation $Y\in\mathcal Y$, and transition law $W(y_r,y\mid x,x_r)$. For a positive integer message-set size $M$, the one-way message is uniform on $[M]$ and the destination estimates it from $Y^n$.

In the **relay-only causal model**, $X_i=f_i(M)$ and $X_{r,i}=g_i(Y_r^{i-1})$. In the **full output-feedback model**, both encoders know the past pair $(Y^{i-1},Y_r^{i-1})$, so $X_i=f_i(M,Y^{i-1},Y_r^{i-1})$ and $X_{r,i}=g_i(Y^{i-1},Y_r^{i-1})$. In either model the channel outputs at time $i$ are drawn from $W(\cdot,\cdot\mid X_i,X_{r,i})$; no encoder sees a current-time output before choosing its current input. The rate is $n^{-1}\ln M$, and achievability uses average error under the uniform message law.

Let $p_{XYZ}$ be a joint probability vector on finite alphabets and write $p_Z(z)$ for its marginal. It is the law of finite coordinate random elements on the canonical finite probability space from [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]] and [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]. For each $z$ with $p_Z(z)>0$, the conditional law $p_{XY|z}$ and its marginals $p_{X|z},p_{Y|z}$ are probability vectors by [[lem-it-finite-marginals-and-conditionals-are-pmfs]]. Define conditional mutual information in nats by

$$I(X;Y|Z):=\sum_{z:p_Z(z)>0}p_Z(z)D(p_{XY|z}\|p_{X|z}\otimes p_{Y|z}),$$

using the finite KL convention of [[def-qa-35-finite-probability-entropy-and-stochastic-matrices]], where $(p_{X|z}\otimes p_{Y|z})(x,y):=p_{X|z}(x)p_{Y|z}(y)$. A positive conditional joint mass forces both conditional marginals to be positive, so each displayed KL term is finite. Zero-mass conditioning values contribute no term. The base-$b$ version replaces $\ln$ by $\log_b$ inside the conditional KL sums.

For finite $X,Y,Z$,

$$I(X;Y|Z)=H(X|Z)+H(Y|Z)-H(X,Y|Z)\ge0.$$

Equality holds if and only if, for every $z$ with $p_Z(z)>0$, the conditional joint pmf factors as $p_{XY|z}=p_{X|z}p_{Y|z}$; this is conditional independence given $Z$.

For finite $X,Y,Z$ with a joint pmf,

$$H(X,Y|Z)=H(X|Z)+H(Y|X,Z),$$

and

$$I(X;Y,Z)=I(X;Z)+I(X;Y|Z).$$

In particular, $I(X;Y)=H(X)-H(X|Y)=H(Y)-H(Y|X)$. All terms are finite.

derivations.claim: Substitute $A=\{s\}$ and $A=\{s,r\}$ into [F1]. The first cut has no source-side reconstruction penalty because the source reconstruction can be constant; the second cut has only the relay penalty $I(Y_r;\hat Y_r|X,X_r,Y)$. These substitutions give the displayed NNC minimum.

The test-channel Markov relation $\hat Y_r-Y_r-(X,Y)$ conditional on $X_r$ gives $$I(Y_r;\hat Y_r|X_r,Y)=I(X;\hat Y_r|X_r,Y)+I(Y_r;\hat Y_r|X,X_r,Y).$$ Indeed, expand $I(X,Y_r;\hat Y_r|X_r,Y)$ in both orders; the term $I(X;\hat Y_r|Y_r,X_r,Y)$ is zero by the test-channel factorization.

Subtract the first NNC term from the second and use [F3]: $$I(X,X_r;Y)-I(Y_r;\hat Y_r|X,X_r,Y)-I(X;Y,\hat Y_r|X_r)=I(X_r;Y)-I(Y_r;\hat Y_r|X_r,Y).$$ Thus the stated compress-forward condition makes the second term at least the first. Thus [F1] proves the asserted positive-rate achievability.
At $R=0$, choose a singleton message set at the source and let the destination return its sole message. This achieves zero error without needing either strict mutual-information inequality.

A **finite two-way relay channel** is the three-node DMN of [[def-finite-discrete-memoryless-network-and-code]] with terminal inputs $X_1,X_2$, relay input $X_r$, terminal outputs $Y_1,Y_2$, relay observation $Y_r$, and transition law $W(y_1,y_2,y_r\mid x_1,x_2,x_r)$. A causal code uses $X_{1,i}=f_{1,i}(M_1,Y_1^{i-1})$, $X_{2,i}=f_{2,i}(M_2,Y_2^{i-1})$, and $X_{r,i}=f_{r,i}(Y_r^{i-1})$; terminal 1 estimates $M_2$ from $(M_1,Y_1^n)$ and terminal 2 estimates $M_1$ from $(M_2,Y_2^n)$. The probability of error is the probability either estimate is wrong. This is a full-duplex model: all three nodes choose an input at every use, and each input depends only on that node's message and past observations.

Let $p_{XYZ}$ be a joint probability vector on finite alphabets and write $p_Z(z)$ for its marginal. It is the law of finite coordinate random elements on the canonical finite probability space from [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]] and [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]. For finite $X,Y,Z$,

$$I(X;Y|Z)=H(X|Z)+H(Y|Z)-H(X,Y|Z)\ge0.$$

Equality holds if and only if, for every $z$ with $p_Z(z)>0$, the conditional joint pmf factors as $p_{XY|z}=p_{X|z}p_{Y|z}$; this is conditional independence given $Z$.

For finite $X,Y,Z$ with a joint pmf,

$$H(X,Y|Z)=H(X|Z)+H(Y|X,Z),$$

and

$$I(X;Y,Z)=I(X;Z)+I(X;Y|Z).$$

In particular, $I(X;Y)=H(X)-H(X|Y)=H(Y)-H(Y|X)$. All terms are finite.

derivations.claim: For destination 2 and message source 1, the cut containing only node 1 yields $I(X_1;Y_2,\hat Y_r|X_2,X_r)$; the cut containing nodes 1 and $r$ yields $I(X_1,X_r;Y_2|X_2)-I(Y_r;\hat Y_r|X_1,X_2,X_r,Y_2)$. The other node's observation reconstruction may be constant. These are the two bounds on $R_1$.

For destination 1 and message source 2, the two cuts are respectively node 2 alone and nodes 2 with the relay. Substitution into [F1] yields the displayed two bounds on $R_2$. Both destinations can use their own message as side information, as in [F2].

Taking the intersection of the two destination constraints and then closure over rates yields the stated inner region; the finite mutual-information quantities use the chain-rule and conditional-law conventions of [F3]. The simultaneous multicast code supplied by [F1] serves both destinations, with each terminal using its own message as side information.

If $R_1=R_2=0$, both terminals use singleton message sets and return their unique required messages, so the error probability is zero. This includes the zero-rate pair even if a displayed right-hand side is negative.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.
Every finite product of standard Borel spaces, with its finite product sigma-algebra, is standard Borel.

For standard-Borel random elements X,Y,Z,
$$I((Z,X);Y)=I(Z;Y)+I(X;Y\mid Z).$$
The right side is a sum in $[0,+\infty]$. This chain rule is asserted as an equality of extended nonnegative quantities; no difference of possibly infinite entropies or divergences occurs.

Assume AC. Let X,Y,Z be random elements with standard-Borel value spaces and write $P_{ZXY}$ for the joint law of $(Z,X,Y)$ in that coordinate order. Let $K(z,\cdot)$ and $L(z,\cdot)$ be regular conditional laws of X and Y given Z=z. Let R be the probability law on the same product space whose rectangle values are
$$R(C\times A\times B)=\int_C K(z,A)L(z,B)\,P_Z(dz).$$
Its existence, uniqueness, and independence of the versions K,L are established in [[lem-same-marginal-conditional-product-law-well-defined]]. Define the **conditional mutual information** by
$$I(X;Y\mid Z):=D(P_{ZXY}\|R)\in[0,+\infty].$$
The reference R has the same Z marginal as the joint law and makes X,Y independent conditionally on Z. The logarithm is natural, so finite values are measured in nats under [[def-it-information-units-and-logarithm-base]]. The definition is a divergence between full probability laws; it does not subtract two possibly infinite entropies.

Let $E,F$ be standard-Borel spaces, let $\mu,
u$ be probability measures on E, and let $K,L:Eightsquigarrow F$ be probability kernels. Let $P=\mu\ltimes K$ and $Q=
u\ltimes L$ be the joint probability laws defined by
$$P(C)=\int_E K(x,C_x)\,\mu(dx),\qquad Q(C)=\int_E L(x,C_x)\,
u(dx)$$
for product-measurable $C\subseteq E	imes F$. Then
$$D(P\|Q)=D(\mu\|
u)+\int_E D(K(x,\cdot)\|L(x,\cdot))\,\mu(dx)=D(\mu\|
u)+D_\mu(K\|L),$$
as an equality in $[0,+\infty]$. In particular, when $\mu=
u$, the joint KL is the conditional KL from [[def-conditional-kl-for-probability-kernels]].

Assume AC and use the directional convention of
[[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. For probability measures $P,Q$ on one
measurable space, $D(P\|Q)\ge0$, and $D(P\|Q)=0$ if and only if $P=Q$.

There is also the following normalized-density identity. Let
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space: it is a set
with a sigma-algebra and measure ([[def-measure-space]]), and there is a
countable measurable cover by sets of finite $\mu$-measure
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]). Let
$\gamma:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable function with
$Z:=\int\gamma\,d\mu\in(0,\infty)$, and put $\pi=\gamma/Z$. Let
$q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable probability density,
so $\int q\,d\mu=1$, and suppose $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on
$\{\gamma=0\}$. Assume
$$\int q\bigl(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|\bigr)\,d\mu<\infty,$$
where each term with $q=0$ is defined to be zero. Then
$$\log Z =\int q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu +D(q\,\mu\|\pi\,\mu).$$
In particular, the first integral is at most $\log Z$. This identity concerns
normalized densities only; it does not assert posterior existence for an
unspecified statistical model.

Let $\phi:(E,\mathcal E)\to(F,\mathcal F)$ be a measurable bijection with measurable inverse. For probability measures P,Q on E, let $\phi_\#P,\phi_\#Q$ be their push-forwards. Then
$$D(\phi_\#P\|\phi_\#Q)=D(P\|Q).$$

derivations.claim: By [F2], successively adjoining $Y_i$ to $Y^{i-1}$ gives $$I(X^n;Y^n)=I(Y^n;X^n)=\sum_{i=1}^n I(Y_i;X^n|Y^{i-1})=\sum_{i=1}^n I(X^n;Y_i|Y^{i-1}).$$ The first equality and the last equality use the coordinate swap in [F5]; the initial term for the empty tuple $Y^0$ is zero. Every term is an extended nonnegative quantity, so no subtraction of infinities is involved.

Fix $i$ and put $U=X_i$, $V=X_{[n]\setminus\{i\}}$, and $W=Y^{i-1}$. For $P_W$-almost every $w$, the conditional channel law makes $Y_i$ independent of $V$ given $U$. Apply [F2] to the conditional law of $(U,V,Y_i)$ given $W=w$ and use [F3]: $$I((U,V);Y_i|W=w)=I(U;Y_i|W=w)+I(V;Y_i|U,W=w)=I(U;Y_i|W=w).$$ Integrating this identity over $P_W$ gives $I(X^n;Y_i|Y^{i-1})=I(X_i;Y_i|Y^{i-1})$ by [F6] and the conditional-KL definition [F3].

The product channel law gives $I(Y^{i-1};Y_i|X_i)=0$ by [F3]. Expanding $I((X_i,Y^{i-1});Y_i)$ with [F2] first in the order $X_i,Y^{i-1}$ gives $I((X_i,Y^{i-1});Y_i)=I(X_i;Y_i)$. Expanding in the reverse order and using the coordinate-swap invariance [F5] gives $$I(X_i;Y_i)=I(Y^{i-1};Y_i)+I(X_i;Y_i|Y^{i-1}).$$ Because the omitted term $I(Y^{i-1};Y_i|X_i)$ is zero and $I(Y^{i-1};Y_i)\ge0$ by [F4], this proves $I(X_i;Y_i|Y^{i-1})\le I(X_i;Y_i)$ in the extended nonnegative order.

Sum the coordinate inequalities from step 1.3 and use the chain-rule expansion in step 1.1 together with step 1.2. This gives $I(X^n;Y^n)\le\sum_{i=1}^nI(X_i;Y_i)$ for arbitrary dependent input coordinates.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The two-user Gaussian interference channel has independent messages, separate encoders, and outputs
$$Y_1=h_{11}X_1+h_{21}X_2+Z_1,\qquad Y_2=h_{12}X_1+h_{22}X_2+Z_2.$$
For the **real model**, $X_i,h_{ji},Z_j$ are real and $Z_j\sim N(0,1)$. For the **complex model**, the inputs and gains are complex and $Z_j\sim\mathcal{CN}(0,1)$ with density $\pi^{-1}e^{-|z|^2}$. The receiver-noise variables are independent across receivers and channel uses and independent of the messages, so the channel is memoryless. Each power budget satisfies $P_i\ge0$. A length-$n$ code has independent uniform messages $M_i$ on $[m_i]$ for integers $m_i\ge1$, deterministic separate encoders $X_i^n=f_i(M_i)$, and decoders $\widehat M_i=g_i(Y_i^n)$; no feedback is present. The expected average-power constraints are $n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^n\mathbb E[X_{i,t}^2]\le P_i$ in the real model and $n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^n\mathbb E|X_{i,t}|^2\le P_i$ in the complex model, with expectations under the uniform message law. The average joint error is $\Pr\{(\widehat M_1,\widehat M_2)\ne(M_1,M_2)\}$. For either model define
$$\mathrm{SNR}_1=|h_{11}|^2P_1,\quad \mathrm{SNR}_2=|h_{22}|^2P_2,\quad \mathrm{INR}_1=|h_{21}|^2P_2,\quad \mathrm{INR}_2=|h_{12}|^2P_1.$$
Rates are bits per use, $R_i=n^{-1}\log_2m_i$. For a scalar unit-noise AWGN link $Y=aX+Z$ with power constraint $P$, the capacity is $\kappa\log_2(1+|a|^2P)$, attained by a centered real Gaussian input or a circular complex Gaussian input; $\kappa=1/2$ in the real model and $\kappa=1$ in the complex model.

Let $M$ be uniform on a finite message set $\mathcal M$ of size $m\ge2$, let $S$ take values in a finite set $\mathcal S$, and let $Y$ take values in $\mathbb R^d$; a complex observation space $\mathbb C^k$ is identified with $\mathbb R^{2k}$. Suppose $Y\mid(M,S)$ has a Lebesgue density. For every measurable estimator $\widehat M=\phi(Y,S)$ with $\phi:\mathbb R^d\times\mathcal S\to\mathcal M$ and error probability $\epsilon$, define $H(M\mid Y,S):=\int H(p_{M|y,s})\,dP_{Y,S}(y,s)$ using its finite posterior vector. Then
$$H(M\mid Y,S)\le h_b(\epsilon)+\epsilon\ln(m-1)\le\ln2+\epsilon\ln m,$$
where $h_b(t)=-t\ln t-(1-t)\ln(1-t)$ and $0\ln0=0$. For $m=1$, the conditional entropy is zero.

Assume AC. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ and $Y_1,\ldots,Y_n$ take values in standard-Borel spaces. Let their joint law have an arbitrary input marginal $P_{X^n}$ and the memoryless conditional channel law
$$P_{Y^n|X^n}(dy^n|x^n)=\prod_{i=1}^n W_i(dy_i|x_i),$$
where each $W_i$ is a probability kernel. No independence across the input coordinates is assumed. Then, as an inequality in $[0,+\infty]$,
$$I(X^n;Y^n)\le\sum_{i=1}^n I(X_i;Y_i).$$

Assume AC. Let $U,V,Y,S$ take values in standard-Borel spaces. Then
$$I((U,V);Y|S)=I(U;Y|S)+I(V;Y|U,S)$$
and also
$$I((U,V);Y|S)=I(V;Y|S)+I(U;Y|V,S),$$
where these are equalities of extended nonnegative quantities. In particular, if the conditional law of $Y$ given $(U,V,S)$ depends only on $(V,S)$, then
$$I(U;Y|S)\le I(V;Y|S).$$

Assume AC. Let $X$ be real or complex with finite second moment, let $Z$ be independent unit-variance Gaussian noise, and let $Y=aX+Z$. In the real case take $Z\sim N(0,1)$ and $a\in\mathbb R$; in the complex case take $Z\sim\mathcal{CN}(0,1)$ with density $\pi^{-1}e^{-|z|^2}$ and $a\in\mathbb C$. Put $v=\mathbb E|X-\mathbb EX|^2$ and $\kappa=1/2$ in the real case, $\kappa=1$ in the complex case. Then
$$I(X;Y)\le\kappa\ln(1+|a|^2v)\le\kappa\ln(1+|a|^2\mathbb E|X|^2)$$
in nats; division by $\ln2$ gives the corresponding bit formula.
Equality in the first inequality holds when $X$ is Gaussian in the real case or circular complex Gaussian in the complex case, including the zero-variance case.

Assume AC, use base-two entropy, and let $Z^n,W^n$ be IID unit circular Gaussian vectors independent of $X^n$, where $n^{-1}\sum_j\operatorname{Var}(X_j)\le P$. For $s\ge t\ge0$,
$$h(\sqrt{s}X^n+Z^n)-h(\sqrt{t}X^n+W^n)\le n\log_2\frac{1+sP}{1+tP}.$$
For the complex channel in [[def-real-two-user-gaussian-interference-channel]], let the two input vectors be independent, obey the average power constraints, and have arbitrary dependence within each vector. Write $a=\mathrm{SNR}_1$, $b=\mathrm{SNR}_2$, $c=\mathrm{INR}_1$, $d=\mathrm{INR}_2$, $S_1^n=h_{12}X_1^n+Z_2^n$, and $S_2^n=h_{21}X_2^n+Z_1^n$. Then
$$h(Y_1^n|S_1^n)\le n\log_2\!\left(\pi e\left[1+c+\frac{a}{1+d}\right]\right),\quad h(Y_2^n|S_2^n)\le n\log_2\!\left(\pi e\left[1+d+\frac{b}{1+c}\right]\right),$$
$$h(Y_1^n)\le n\log_2(\pi e[1+a+c]),\quad h(Y_2^n)\le n\log_2(\pi e[1+b+d]),$$
$$h(Y_2^n|S_2^n,X_1^n)\le n\log_2\!\left(\pi e\left[1+\frac{b}{1+c}\right]\right),$$
and the index-reflected conditional bound also holds.

derivations.claim: Write $a=\mathrm{SNR}_1$, $b=\mathrm{SNR}_2$, $c=\mathrm{INR}_1$, $d=\mathrm{INR}_2$. Give $M_2$ to receiver 1 and subtract its deterministic codeword. Fano, conditional data processing in both directions, and tensorization give $nR_1\le\sum_j I(X_{1,j};h_{11}X_{1,j}+Z_{1,j})+o(n)$. The scalar Gaussian power bound followed by Jensen and the average input constraint gives $R_1\le\log_2(1+a)$. Reflection gives $R_2\le\log_2(1+b)$. The same argument applies when a direct gain vanishes and then forces the corresponding rate to zero. Throughout the proof independent messages give independent user input vectors, regardless of coordinate dependence inside a vector; the additive Fano remainders disappear on division by $n$ and passage to the coding limit.

Reveal $X_2^n$ to receiver 1. The chain rule and independent inputs give the following exact expansion of the two augmented mutual informations: $I(X_1^n;Y_1^n|X_2^n)+I(X_2^n;Y_2^n)=h(Y_2^n)-h(Z_1^n)+h(h_{11}X_1^n+Z_1^n)-h(h_{12}X_1^n+Z_2^n)$. If $P_1=0$, the input vector is zero and this entropy difference and the claimed logarithmic ratio are both zero. Otherwise, if $a\ge d$, the entropy-difference estimate [F6] applies with $s=|h_{11}|^2$, $t=|h_{12}|^2$, $P=P_1$; phases are removed by unit-modulus rotations. This is precisely the coupling condition $|h_{11}|\ge|h_{12}|$: the lower-SNR observation can be formed by scaling the higher-SNR observation and adding circular Gaussian noise of variance $1-t/s$. The proof of [F6] covers zero gains without division by a cross gain. Its unconditioned-output bound therefore yields $R_1+R_2\le\log_2(1+b+d)+\log_2((1+a)/(1+d))=\log_2(1+a)+\log_2(1+b/(1+d))$. Only $a\ge d$ is needed. Reflecting the argument gives the second weak sum bound under $b\ge c$, using the reflected noise coupling.

Define $S_1^n=h_{12}X_1^n+Z_2^n$ and $S_2^n=h_{21}X_2^n+Z_1^n$ using independent receiver noises. Give $S_1^n$ to receiver 1 and $S_2^n$ to receiver 2. Expanding both augmented informations gives $I(X_1^n;Y_1^n,S_1^n)+I(X_2^n;Y_2^n,S_2^n)=h(Y_1^n|S_1^n)+h(Y_2^n|S_2^n)-h(Z_1^n)-h(Z_2^n)$: the positive $h(S_1^n)$ and $h(S_2^n)$ cancel the interference-plus-noise entropies of the two conditional channels. Applying the two conditional-output estimates in [F6] and $h(Z_i^n)=n\log_2(\pi e)$ proves the third displayed weak sum bound. This calculation is valid in every regime and requires no degradation inequality.

Add two copies of receiver 1's Fano bound and one of receiver 2's. Augment receiver 2 by $S_2^n$ and one receiver 1 copy by $X_2^n$. The resulting information sum equals $h(Y_1^n)+h(Y_2^n|S_2^n)-2h(Z_1^n)+h(h_{11}X_1^n+Z_1^n)-h(h_{12}X_1^n+Z_2^n)$. Indeed the three information terms contribute, respectively, $h(Y_1^n)-h(S_2^n)$, $h(S_2^n)+h(Y_2^n|S_2^n)-h(h_{12}X_1^n+Z_2^n)-h(Z_1^n)$, and $h(h_{11}X_1^n+Z_1^n)-h(Z_1^n)$. The unconditioned, conditional, and entropy-difference estimates of [F6] give $2R_1+R_2\le\log_2(1+a+c)+\log_2(1+d+b/(1+c))+\log_2((1+a)/(1+d))$. The only degradation hypothesis is $a\ge d$, exactly as in step 2.1. Reflection proves the displayed $R_1+2R_2$ bound under $b\ge c$. Thus the stated weak regime supplies every required coupling.

In the mixed regime $c\ge b$ and $a>d$, the individual bounds and first sum bound still follow from steps 1.1 and 2.1. For the MAC sum bound, receiver 1 first decodes $M_1$. On the event of correct decoding it subtracts $h_{11}X_1^n$ and obtains $h_{21}X_2^n+Z_1^n$. If $P_2=0$, step 1.1 gives $R_2=0$ and the required MAC sum bound already follows from the individual bound. Otherwise, if $h_{21}\ne0$, scale by $h_{22}/h_{21}$ and add independent circular Gaussian noise of variance $1-|h_{22}/h_{21}|^2$, which is nonnegative because $c\ge b$ and $P_2>0$. Add the known vector $h_{12}X_1^n$ and apply receiver 2's decoder. Coupling this simulation to the one using the true $M_1$ bounds its joint-message error by the sum of the two original errors; a deterministic MAP decoder has no larger average error. Joint-message Fano and the unconditioned-output estimate [F6] give $R_1+R_2\le\log_2(1+a+c)$. If $h_{21}=0$, then $b=c=0$ and step 1.1 forces $R_2=0$, so the same sum bound follows immediately. This establishes the exact mixed sum claim, including degenerate gains.

For the mixed weighted bound add the three Fano information terms $I(X_1^n;Y_1^n,S_1^n)$, $I(X_2^n;Y_2^n)$, and $I(X_2^n;Y_2^n,S_2^n|X_1^n)$. The first expands as $h(S_1^n)-h(Z_2^n)+h(Y_1^n|S_1^n)-h(S_2^n)$, the second as $h(Y_2^n)-h(S_1^n)$, and the third as $h(S_2^n)-h(Z_1^n)+h(Y_2^n|S_2^n,X_1^n)-h(Z_2^n)$. Their sum is $h(Y_1^n|S_1^n)+h(Y_2^n)+h(Y_2^n|S_2^n,X_1^n)-h(Z_1^n)-2h(Z_2^n)$. Apply the three corresponding bounds in [F6] to obtain exactly $R_1+2R_2\le\log_2(1+b+d)+\log_2(1+c+a/(1+d))+\log_2(1+b/(1+c))$. This particular weighted estimate is universal and uses no degradation condition. Reflection gives the other mixed regime. Combining the preceding steps proves every displayed inequality with precisely the hypotheses asserted in the statement.
