A **finite discrete memoryless relay channel** is the three-node instance of [[def-finite-discrete-memoryless-network-and-code]] with source input $X\in\mathcal X$, relay input $X_r\in\mathcal X_r$, relay observation $Y_r\in\mathcal Y_r$, destination observation $Y\in\mathcal Y$, and transition law $W(y_r,y\mid x,x_r)$. For a positive integer message-set size $M$, the one-way message is uniform on $[M]$ and the destination estimates it from $Y^n$.

In the **relay-only causal model**, $X_i=f_i(M)$ and $X_{r,i}=g_i(Y_r^{i-1})$. In the **full output-feedback model**, both encoders know the past pair $(Y^{i-1},Y_r^{i-1})$, so $X_i=f_i(M,Y^{i-1},Y_r^{i-1})$ and $X_{r,i}=g_i(Y^{i-1},Y_r^{i-1})$. In either model the channel outputs at time $i$ are drawn from $W(\cdot,\cdot\mid X_i,X_{r,i})$; no encoder sees a current-time output before choosing its current input. The rate is $n^{-1}\ln M$, and achievability uses average error under the uniform message law.

Let $X$ take values in an alphabet $\mathcal X$ of size $m\ge2$, let $Y$ be finite, and let $\widehat X$ be an estimator in the same alphabet generated from $Y$, so the joint pmf factors as $p_{XY\widehat X}=p_{XY}p_{\widehat X|Y}$. Put $P_e=\mathbb P[\widehat X\ne X]$ and define

$$h_2(t):=-t\ln t-(1-t)\ln(1-t),\qquad 0\ln0:=0.$$

Then

$$H(X|Y)\le h_2(P_e)+P_e\ln(m-1)\le \ln2+P_e\ln m.$$

For $m=1$, $X$ is constant and $H(X|Y)=0$.

For finite $X,Y,Z$,

$$I(X;Y|Z)=H(X|Z)+H(Y|Z)-H(X,Y|Z)\ge0.$$

Equality holds if and only if, for every $z$ with $p_Z(z)>0$, the conditional joint pmf factors as $p_{XY|z}=p_{X|z}p_{Y|z}$; this is conditional independence given $Z$.

For finite $X,Y,Z$ with a joint pmf,

$$H(X,Y|Z)=H(X|Z)+H(Y|X,Z),$$

and

$$I(X;Y,Z)=I(X;Z)+I(X;Y|Z).$$

In particular, $I(X;Y)=H(X)-H(X|Y)=H(Y)-H(Y|X)$. All terms are finite.

Let $Q,X,Z,Y$ be finite random variables and suppose the channel law $P_{Y|X,Z,Q}$ depends on $Q$ only through $(X,Z)$; equivalently, $Q-(X,Z)-Y$ is a Markov chain. Then
$$I(X;Y\mid Z)\ge I(X;Y\mid Z,Q).$$
Thus, for a fixed finite channel and fixed side information $Z$, averaging input laws over a time-sharing variable cannot increase the average conditional mutual information.

derivations.claim: Fano's inequality gives $(1-P_e)\ln|\mathcal M|\le I(M;Y^n)+\ln2$. Apply the chain rule to write $I(M;Y^n)=\sum_i I(M;Y_i\mid Y^{i-1})$.

Since conditional mutual information is nonnegative, each summand is at most $I(M,Y_r^{i-1};Y_i\mid Y^{i-1})$. Given $(M,Y^{i-1},Y_r^{i-1})$, the current inputs are fixed by causality in either model, and [F1] makes the current output depend on those variables only through $(X_i,X_{r,i})$. Thus the summand equals $I(X_i,X_{r,i};Y_i\mid Y^{i-1})$. For the fixed channel $W_Y$, the past $Y^{i-1}$ is a time-sharing variable independent of the current output once the current inputs are fixed. Applying [F5] gives $I(X_i,X_{r,i};Y_i\mid Y^{i-1})\le I(X_i,X_{r,i};Y_i)$.

For the second cut, $I(M;Y^n)\le I(M;Y^n,Y_r^n)=\sum_i I(M;Y_i,Y_{r,i}\mid Y^{i-1},Y_r^{i-1})$. The relay input $X_{r,i}$ is determined by the past. Given the past and $M$, the source input is determined; memorylessness therefore reduces each term to $I(X_i;Y_i,Y_{r,i}\mid Y^{i-1},Y_r^{i-1},X_{r,i})$. Conditional on a fixed $X_{r,i}=x_r$, the past is a time-sharing variable for the fixed channel $W_{(Y,Y_r)|X,x_r}$. Applying [F5] and averaging over $X_{r,i}$ bounds the term by $I(X_i;Y_i,Y_{r,i}\mid X_{r,i})$.

Let $Q$ be uniform on $[n]$ and conditionally draw $(X,X_r,Y_r,Y)$ according to the time-$Q$ joint law induced by the code and channel. Steps 2.1, 2.2 imply both cut inequalities with conditioning on $Q$. Dividing the Fano bound by $n$, then taking a sequence of codes with $P_e\to0$, gives the stated outer bound after closure and convexification.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

All mutual informations and rates in this item are measured in bits; differential entropies in the proof are in nats and are divided by $\ln2$.

In the real Gaussian multicast network of [[def-real-gaussian-multicast-relay-network]], take independent Gaussian inputs $X_i\sim N(0,P_i)$ and independent Gaussian test-channel noises. For a chosen node set $\mathcal Q\subseteq[N]$, set $\hat Y_i=Y_i+\hat Z_i$ with $\hat Z_i\sim N(0,1)$ for $i\in\mathcal Q$ and let $\hat Y_i$ be constant otherwise. Every nonnegative rate tuple satisfying
$$\sum_{k\in A\cap\mathcal S}R_k<I(X_A;Y_d,\hat Y_{A^c\cap\mathcal Q}\mid X_{A^c})-I(Y_{A\cap\mathcal Q};\hat Y_{A\cap\mathcal Q}\mid X_{[N]},Y_d,\hat Y_{A^c\cap\mathcal Q})$$
for every destination $d\in\mathcal D$ and every cut $A\subseteq[N]$ with $d\notin A$ and $A\cap\mathcal S\ne\varnothing$ is achievable under the stated average-power constraints. The closure of the union of these strict regions over the stated choices, together with the all-zero tuple, is achievable.

In the special case $P_i=P>0$ for every node and $\mathcal Q=[N]$, a noise-level evaluation gives the sufficient cut inequalities
$$\sum_{k\in A\cap\mathcal S}R_k < \frac12\log_2\det\!\left(I+\frac P2G(A)G(A)^T\right)-\frac{|A|}{2}$$
for every $A\subseteq[N]$ with $A^c\cap\mathcal D\ne\varnothing$ and $A\cap\mathcal S\ne\varnothing$, where $G(A)=G_{A^c,A}$. Their closure is achievable. The all-zero rate tuple is always achievable by singleton source-message sets, independently of whether these cut right-hand sides are nonnegative.

A **real scalar Gaussian relay network** has node set $[N]$ for an integer $N\ge1$, source set $\mathcal S\subseteq[N]$, destination set $\mathcal D\subseteq[N]$, one real input $X_i$ and output $Y_i$ at each node, and channel equations
$$Y_j=\sum_{i=1}^N g_{ji}X_i+Z_j,\qquad j\in[N],$$
where the gains $g_{ji}\in\mathbb R$ are fixed and the noises $Z_j$ are independent $N(0,1)$ random variables, independent across channel uses and of all source messages. At each use the current noise vector is independent of all past observations and the current inputs; future inputs may depend on past noises through feedback. Each node has a nonnegative power budget $P_i\ge0$ and average power constraint $\frac1n\sum_{t=1}^n\mathbb E[X_{i,t}^2]\le P_i$. Each source $i\in\mathcal S$ has an independent uniform message $M_i$ in a finite nonempty set $\mathcal M_i$. For every non-source node $i\notin\mathcal S$, set $\mathcal M_i=\{*\}$ and $M_i=*$, so its encoder has no message information. A length-$n$ causal code uses measurable encoders $X_{i,t}=f_{i,t}(M_i,Y_i^{t-1})$ and destination decoders based on $(Y_d^n,M_d)$, where $M_d$ is its own source message when $d\in\mathcal S$ and a singleton otherwise; multicast means every destination must decode every other source message, while its own message is already known. The average error probability is the probability that any required destination estimate is wrong. Write $G_{B,A}$ for the matrix with rows indexed by $B$ and columns by $A$ whose entries are $g_{ji}$.

Rates in this page's Gaussian formulas are measured in bits per use, $R_i=n^{-1}\log_2|\mathcal M_i|$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. If a random vector $X\in\mathbb R^d$ has a Lebesgue density, finite mean $m$, positive-definite covariance $K$, and finite differential entropy $h(X)=-\int f\ln f$, then
$$h(X)\le \frac12\ln\bigl((2\pi e)^d\det K\bigr).$$
Equality holds exactly when $X$ has the Gaussian law $N_d(m,K)$.

Let $M$ be uniform on a finite message set $\mathcal M$ of size $m\ge2$, let $S$ take values in a finite set $\mathcal S$, and let $Y$ take values in $\mathbb R^d$; a complex observation space $\mathbb C^k$ is identified with $\mathbb R^{2k}$. Suppose $Y\mid(M,S)$ has a Lebesgue density. For every measurable estimator $\widehat M=\phi(Y,S)$ with $\phi:\mathbb R^d\times\mathcal S\to\mathcal M$ and error probability $\epsilon$, define $H(M\mid Y,S):=\int H(p_{M|y,s})\,dP_{Y,S}(y,s)$ using its finite posterior vector. Then
$$H(M\mid Y,S)\le h_b(\epsilon)+\epsilon\ln(m-1)\le\ln2+\epsilon\ln m,$$
where $h_b(t)=-t\ln t-(1-t)\ln(1-t)$ and $0\ln0=0$. For $m=1$, the conditional entropy is zero.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Assume AC. Let $U,V,Y,S$ take values in standard-Borel spaces. Then
$$I((U,V);Y|S)=I(U;Y|S)+I(V;Y|U,S)$$
and also
$$I((U,V);Y|S)=I(V;Y|S)+I(U;Y|V,S),$$
where these are equalities of extended nonnegative quantities. In particular, if the conditional law of $Y$ given $(U,V,S)$ depends only on $(V,S)$, then
$$I(U;Y|S)\le I(V;Y|S).$$

Let $f$ be a Lebesgue probability density on $\mathbb R^d$ with $\|f\|_\infty<\infty$ and $\int |x|^2f(x)\,dx<\infty$. Then $\int f(x)|\ln f(x)|\,dx<\infty$, so the differential entropy in [[def-it-real-differential-entropy]] is a finite real number.

derivations.claim: Fix a destination $d\in A^c$. Give the messages of nodes in $A^c$ to that destination, and also give it all outputs $Y_{A^c}^n$. The revealed messages are independent of the source messages in $A$, and the original decoder is still available. Since rates are bits and Fano's bound is in nats, [F4] gives the exact finite-code bound $$(1-P_e)n\ln2\sum_{k\in A\cap\mathcal S}R_k^{(n)}\le I(M_{A\cap\mathcal S};Y_{A^c}^n\mid M_{A^c})+\ln2.$$ By the conditional chain rule [F6], expand the mutual information across time. For time $i$, condition on $H_i=(M_{A^c},Y_{A^c}^{i-1})$. Each input in $A^c$ is then fixed by causality in [F2]. The current outputs depend on messages in $A$ only through the current inputs $X_{A,i}$, so conditional data processing [F6] gives $$I(M_{A\cap\mathcal S};Y_{A^c,i}\mid H_i)\le I(X_{A,i};Y_{A^c,i}\mid H_i).$$ The right side is the mutual information of $G(A)X_{A,i}+Z_{A^c,i}$ under the conditional input law given $H_i$.

For almost every $h$, the conditional input second moment given $H_i=h$ is finite, since its average is bounded by the node power constraints. The conditional output is a translate of a Gaussian convolution, so its density is bounded by the standard Gaussian noise peak; [F7] makes its differential entropy finite. Let $K_{i,h}$ be the conditional covariance of $X_{A,i}$ given $H_i=h$. The channel noise is independent with covariance $I$, so [F3] bounds each conditional mutual information in step 1.1, measured in nats, by $$\frac12\ln\det(I_{|A^c|}+G(A)K_{i,h}G(A)^T).$$ Set $\bar K=n^{-1}\sum_i\mathbb E[K_{i,H_i}]$. Since covariance trace is at most the corresponding second moment and each node's average power is at most $P$, $\bar K\succeq0$ and $\operatorname{tr}\bar K\le |A|P$.

For positive-definite matrices $B,B_0$, let $C=B_0^{-1/2}BB_0^{-1/2}$. Its eigenvalues $\lambda_j$ are positive by [F5], and $\ln\lambda_j\le\lambda_j-1$ because $u-1-\ln u$ has derivative $1-1/u$, decreases on $(0,1]$, increases on $[1,\infty)$, and vanishes at $1$. Thus $$\ln\det B\le\ln\det B_0+\operatorname{tr}(B_0^{-1}(B-B_0)).$$ Apply this with $B=I+G K_{i,h}G^T$ and $B_0=I+G\bar K G^T$, then average over $i,h$; the trace term averages to zero. Hence the average natural log determinant in step 2.1 is at most $\ln\det(I+G\bar K G^T)$. The spectral theorem gives $\bar K\preceq\operatorname{tr}(\bar K)I$, since every nonnegative eigenvalue is at most their sum; hence $G\bar K G^T\preceq |A|P GG^T$. If $0\prec C\preceq D$, then $C^{-1/2}DC^{-1/2}=I+E$ for some $E\succeq0$, so its eigenvalues are at least one and $\det C\le\det D$. Applying this order property and dividing the Fano bound in step 1.1 by $n\ln2$ yields $$(1-P_e)\sum_{k\in A\cap\mathcal S}R_k^{(n)}\le\frac{1}{2\ln2}\ln\det(I_{|A^c|}+|A|P GG^T)+\frac1n.$$ Along a sequence of reliable codes $P_e\to0$, this finite bound first bounds the cut rate sums, and then passage to their achievable lower limits gives $$\sum_{k\in A\cap\mathcal S}R_k\le\frac{1}{2\ln2}\ln\det(I_{|A^c|}+|A|P GG^T).$$ No a priori bounded-rate hypothesis is needed.

Put $a=|A|$ and $b=|A^c|$; both are positive. For any positive-semidefinite $H$ of size $m$, $I_m+aPH\preceq2a(I_m+(P/2)H)$, so determinant monotonicity gives $$\frac{1}{2\ln2}\ln\det(I_m+aPH)\le\frac12\log_2\det(I_m+(P/2)H)+\frac m2\log_2(2a).$$ The block determinant of $\begin{pmatrix}I_b&\sqrt{aP}G\\-\sqrt{aP}G^T&I_a\end{pmatrix}$, computed by taking either identity block as the Schur complement pivot, gives $\det(I_b+aPGG^T)=\det(I_a+aPG^TG)$. Apply the previous inequality once in dimension $b$ and once in dimension $a$, then use this identity to take the smaller additive term. The cut-set outer bound is at most $$\frac12\log_2\det\!\left(I+\frac P2GG^T\right)+\frac12\min(a,b)\log_2(2a).$$

Write $D(A)=\frac12\log_2\det(I+(P/2)G(A)G(A)^T)$, so the sufficient lower bound in [F1] is $L(A)=D(A)-a/2$. Step 4.1 gives the cut-set outer value $O(A)\le D(A)+\frac12\min(a,b)\log_2(2a)=L(A)+\Delta(A)$. If $L(A)>0$, the exact NNC expression satisfies $N_d(A)\ge L(A)$, so $O(A)-N_d(A)\le\Delta(A)$. If $L(A)\le0$, use the separately achievable zero-rate tuple from [F1]; then $O(A)\le L(A)+\Delta(A)\le\Delta(A)$, so the outer cut is within $\Delta(A)$ of that achievable rate. This proves the cutwise comparison without treating the determinant expression as the exact NNC rate and covers negative sufficient-cut values.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The two-user Gaussian interference channel has independent messages, separate encoders, and outputs
$$Y_1=h_{11}X_1+h_{21}X_2+Z_1,\qquad Y_2=h_{12}X_1+h_{22}X_2+Z_2.$$
For the **real model**, $X_i,h_{ji},Z_j$ are real and $Z_j\sim N(0,1)$. For the **complex model**, the inputs and gains are complex and $Z_j\sim\mathcal{CN}(0,1)$ with density $\pi^{-1}e^{-|z|^2}$. The receiver-noise variables are independent across receivers and channel uses and independent of the messages, so the channel is memoryless. Each power budget satisfies $P_i\ge0$. A length-$n$ code has independent uniform messages $M_i$ on $[m_i]$ for integers $m_i\ge1$, deterministic separate encoders $X_i^n=f_i(M_i)$, and decoders $\widehat M_i=g_i(Y_i^n)$; no feedback is present. The expected average-power constraints are $n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^n\mathbb E[X_{i,t}^2]\le P_i$ in the real model and $n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^n\mathbb E|X_{i,t}|^2\le P_i$ in the complex model, with expectations under the uniform message law. The average joint error is $\Pr\{(\widehat M_1,\widehat M_2)\ne(M_1,M_2)\}$. For either model define
$$\mathrm{SNR}_1=|h_{11}|^2P_1,\quad \mathrm{SNR}_2=|h_{22}|^2P_2,\quad \mathrm{INR}_1=|h_{21}|^2P_2,\quad \mathrm{INR}_2=|h_{12}|^2P_1.$$
Rates are bits per use, $R_i=n^{-1}\log_2m_i$. For a scalar unit-noise AWGN link $Y=aX+Z$ with power constraint $P$, the capacity is $\kappa\log_2(1+|a|^2P)$, attained by a centered real Gaussian input or a circular complex Gaussian input; $\kappa=1/2$ in the real model and $\kappa=1$ in the complex model.

At either receiver of the Gaussian channel in [[def-real-two-user-gaussian-interference-channel]], independent Gaussian codebooks with powers $P_1,P_2$ achieve every nonnegative rate pair for which each nonempty subset $T\subseteq\{1,2\}$ with $\sum_{i\in T}R_i>0$ satisfies
$$\sum_{i\in T}R_i<\kappa\log_2\!\left(1+\sum_{i\in T}|a_i|^2P_i\right),$$
where that receiver observes $Y=a_1X_1+a_2X_2+Z$ with unit-variance real or complex Gaussian noise and $\kappa=1/2$ or $1$, respectively. The codebook symbols are centered $N(0,P_i)$ in the real model and circular $\mathcal{CN}(0,P_i)$ in the complex model. A subset of zero total rate has no false-message candidates and requires no strict inequality; in particular the zero pair is achieved by singleton message sets. The closure of this achievable set is the usual closed Gaussian multiple-access region.

Let $M$ be uniform on a finite message set $\mathcal M$ of size $m\ge2$, let $S$ take values in a finite set $\mathcal S$, and let $Y$ take values in $\mathbb R^d$; a complex observation space $\mathbb C^k$ is identified with $\mathbb R^{2k}$. Suppose $Y\mid(M,S)$ has a Lebesgue density. For every measurable estimator $\widehat M=\phi(Y,S)$ with $\phi:\mathbb R^d\times\mathcal S\to\mathcal M$ and error probability $\epsilon$, define $H(M\mid Y,S):=\int H(p_{M|y,s})\,dP_{Y,S}(y,s)$ using its finite posterior vector. Then
$$H(M\mid Y,S)\le h_b(\epsilon)+\epsilon\ln(m-1)\le\ln2+\epsilon\ln m,$$
where $h_b(t)=-t\ln t-(1-t)\ln(1-t)$ and $0\ln0=0$. For $m=1$, the conditional entropy is zero.

Assume AC. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ and $Y_1,\ldots,Y_n$ take values in standard-Borel spaces. Let their joint law have an arbitrary input marginal $P_{X^n}$ and the memoryless conditional channel law
$$P_{Y^n|X^n}(dy^n|x^n)=\prod_{i=1}^n W_i(dy_i|x_i),$$
where each $W_i$ is a probability kernel. No independence across the input coordinates is assumed. Then, as an inequality in $[0,+\infty]$,
$$I(X^n;Y^n)\le\sum_{i=1}^n I(X_i;Y_i).$$

Assume AC. Let $U,V,Y,S$ take values in standard-Borel spaces. Then
$$I((U,V);Y|S)=I(U;Y|S)+I(V;Y|U,S)$$
and also
$$I((U,V);Y|S)=I(V;Y|S)+I(U;Y|V,S),$$
where these are equalities of extended nonnegative quantities. In particular, if the conditional law of $Y$ given $(U,V,S)$ depends only on $(V,S)$, then
$$I(U;Y|S)\le I(V;Y|S).$$

Assume AC. Let $X$ be real or complex with finite second moment, let $Z$ be independent unit-variance Gaussian noise, and let $Y=aX+Z$. In the real case take $Z\sim N(0,1)$ and $a\in\mathbb R$; in the complex case take $Z\sim\mathcal{CN}(0,1)$ with density $\pi^{-1}e^{-|z|^2}$ and $a\in\mathbb C$. Put $v=\mathbb E|X-\mathbb EX|^2$ and $\kappa=1/2$ in the real case, $\kappa=1$ in the complex case. Then
$$I(X;Y)\le\kappa\ln(1+|a|^2v)\le\kappa\ln(1+|a|^2\mathbb E|X|^2)$$
in nats; division by $\ln2$ gives the corresponding bit formula.
Equality in the first inequality holds when $X$ is Gaussian in the real case or circular complex Gaussian in the complex case, including the zero-variance case.

derivations.claim: For the individual bound on $R_1$, give $M_2$ to receiver 1. Fano gives $nR_1\ln2\le I(M_1;Y_1^n|M_2)+o(n)$ in nats. For each fixed $M_2$, $X_2^n$ is fixed; translating $Y_1^n$ by the known vector $-h_{21}X_2^n$ is invertible, so [F5] in both directions preserves this conditional mutual information. The shifted channel from $X_1^n$ is memoryless. The codeword map is deterministic and the channel law depends on $M_1$ only through $X_1^n$, so [F5] in both Markov directions gives $I(M_1;Y_1^n|M_2)=I(X_1^n;h_{11}X_1^n+Z_1^n|M_2)$. Apply [F4] for each $M_2$ and average to bound this by $\sum_iI(X_{1,i};h_{11}X_{1,i}+Z_{1,i})$. By [F6], each term is at most $\kappa\ln(1+|h_{11}|^2p_{1,i})$ nats, where $p_{1,i}=\mathbb E|X_{1,i}|^2$. Jensen's inequality and the power constraint give $R_1\le\kappa\log_2(1+\mathrm{SNR}_1)$. Exchanging users gives the stated $R_2$ bound.

First suppose both cross gains are nonzero. Receiver 1 first forms its estimate $\widehat M_1$. On the event $\widehat M_1=M_1$, it reconstructs $X_1^n$ and subtracts $h_{11}X_1^n$, obtaining $h_{21}X_2^n+Z_1^n$. Since $|h_{21}|\ge|h_{22}|$, it scales this residual by $h_{22}/h_{21}$ and adds independent Gaussian noise of variance $1-|h_{22}/h_{21}|^2$; for complex channels use circular Gaussian noise. Adding back $h_{12}X_1^n$ gives a simulated $\widetilde Y_2^n$. For the error analysis, construct the same vector using the true $M_1$: it then has exactly the law of receiver 2's $Y_2^n$, and on $\widehat M_1=M_1$ it equals the receiver's simulation. Hence the joint error is at most $P_{e,1}+P_{e,2}$. Since the message pair is finite, the randomized decoder has a deterministic MAP decoder with no larger average error. Exchanging users and using $|h_{12}|\ge|h_{11}|$ gives the symmetric joint decoder at receiver 2.

In the nonzero-cross-gain case of step 1.2, apply the density-observation Fano bound [F3] to the joint decoder at receiver 1. Let $M=(M_1,M_2)$ and $X=(X_1^n,X_2^n)$. The deterministic codeword map and channel law give both Markov directions between $M$ and $X$ with observation $Y_1^n$, so [F5] yields $I(M;Y_1^n)=I(X;Y_1^n)$. The two input vectors are independent because their messages are independent. By [F4], $n(R_1+R_2)\ln2\le I(X_1^n,X_2^n;Y_1^n)+o(n)\le\sum_iI(X_{1,i},X_{2,i};Y_{1,i})+o(n)$. The output variance at time $i$ is at most $1+|h_{11}|^2\mathbb E|X_{1,i}|^2+|h_{21}|^2\mathbb E|X_{2,i}|^2$, because the independent inputs have zero cross covariance after centering. These single-coordinate mutual informations are finite by the power bound and [F6].

For each coordinate put $S_i=h_{11}X_{1,i}+h_{21}X_{2,i}$. The channel output depends on the input pair only through $S_i$, so [F5] in both directions gives $I(X_{1,i},X_{2,i};Y_{1,i})=I(S_i;S_i+Z_{1,i})$. Independence gives $\operatorname{Var}(S_i)\le |h_{11}|^2p_{1,i}+|h_{21}|^2p_{2,i}$; [F6] therefore bounds this term by $\kappa\ln(1+|h_{11}|^2p_{1,i}+|h_{21}|^2p_{2,i})$ nats. Jensen's inequality and the average power constraints yield $R_1+R_2\le\kappa\log_2(1+\mathrm{SNR}_1+\mathrm{INR}_1)$. The joint decoder at receiver 2 analogously gives $R_1+R_2\le\kappa\log_2(1+\mathrm{SNR}_2+\mathrm{INR}_2)$. If $h_{21}=0$, then $h_{22}=0$, so $R_2=0$ by step 1.1; the first sum bound is the $R_1$ individual bound and the second is no tighter because $\mathrm{INR}_2\ge\mathrm{SNR}_1$. If $h_{12}=0$, then $h_{11}=0$, so $R_1=0$ and the second sum bound is the $R_2$ individual bound while the first is no tighter because $\mathrm{INR}_1\ge\mathrm{SNR}_2$. Thus both sum bounds hold also when a cross gain vanishes.

Use the same independent Gaussian codebook ensemble at the two receivers. The finite-receiver construction in the proof of [F2] sums the two ensemble-average errors and jointly selects codebooks meeting both deterministic power constraints, so one codebook pair achieves the intersection of the two Gaussian MAC regions. The strong gain inequalities make each unintended-receiver individual constraint at least as large as the corresponding intended-receiver constraint; the two sum constraints are exactly those displayed. Therefore every rate pair strictly inside the claimed region is achievable, and closure removes strictness.

A **finite discrete memoryless relay channel** is the three-node instance of [[def-finite-discrete-memoryless-network-and-code]] with source input $X\in\mathcal X$, relay input $X_r\in\mathcal X_r$, relay observation $Y_r\in\mathcal Y_r$, destination observation $Y\in\mathcal Y$, and transition law $W(y_r,y\mid x,x_r)$. For a positive integer message-set size $M$, the one-way message is uniform on $[M]$ and the destination estimates it from $Y^n$.

In the **relay-only causal model**, $X_i=f_i(M)$ and $X_{r,i}=g_i(Y_r^{i-1})$. In the **full output-feedback model**, both encoders know the past pair $(Y^{i-1},Y_r^{i-1})$, so $X_i=f_i(M,Y^{i-1},Y_r^{i-1})$ and $X_{r,i}=g_i(Y^{i-1},Y_r^{i-1})$. In either model the channel outputs at time $i$ are drawn from $W(\cdot,\cdot\mid X_i,X_{r,i})$; no encoder sees a current-time output before choosing its current input. The rate is $n^{-1}\ln M$, and achievability uses average error under the uniform message law.

For either causal model in [[def-finite-discrete-memoryless-relay-channel-and-causal-code]], every achievable rate is in the closed convex hull of rate values satisfying, for some finite time-sharing variable $Q$ and law $P_QP_{XX_r|Q}$,
$$R\le I(X,X_r;Y\mid Q),\qquad R\le I(X;Y,Y_r\mid X_r,Q),$$
with the relay transition law used to evaluate the mutual informations. In particular, this is an outer bound; it need not be achievable for relay-only causality.

For a finite relay channel with relay-only causality, fix a finite law $P_{X_r}P_{X\mid X_r}$. Every positive rate
$$0<R<\min\{I(X;Y_r\mid X_r),\ I(X,X_r;Y)\}$$
is achievable, and rate $R=0$ is always achievable with a one-message code. Taking the closure of the union over such laws gives the decode-forward inner bound. Mutual informations use the relay channel law and nats per use.

For a finite nonempty set identified with $[k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}$, a **probability vector** is $p=(p_i)_{i=1}^k$ with $p_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i p_i=1$; it is the outcome-weight vector of a finite probability space ([[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]). Its Shannon entropy in natural units is
$$H(p):=-\sum_{i=1}^k p_i\ln p_i,$$
with $0\ln0:=0$. For probability vectors $p,q$ on the same set $[k]$, the relative entropy is
$$D(p\|q):=\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\ln(p_i/q_i),$$
with value $+\infty$ if $p_i>0=q_i$ for some $i$. A matrix $A\in[0,1]^{N\times m}$ is **row-stochastic** when each row sums to one. For a probability row vector $p$ on $[m]$ and a row vector $X\in[0,1]^m$, the dot product $pX^{\mathsf T}=\sum_{i=1}^m p_iX_i$ is the acceptance probability under distribution $p$.

These definitions use finite sets only; entropy is between $0$ and $\ln k$, as proved where needed below.

Let $Q,X,Z,Y$ be finite random variables and suppose the channel law $P_{Y|X,Z,Q}$ depends on $Q$ only through $(X,Z)$; equivalently, $Q-(X,Z)-Y$ is a Markov chain. Then
$$I(X;Y\mid Z)\ge I(X;Y\mid Z,Q).$$
Thus, for a fixed finite channel and fixed side information $Z$, averaging input laws over a time-sharing variable cannot increase the average conditional mutual information.

derivations.claim: Apply [F2]. Its outer bound has a finite time-sharing variable $Q$ and bounds $I(X,X_r;Y|Q)$ and $I(X;Y,Y_r|X_r,Q)$. Apply [F5] first with input $(X,X_r)$ and no side information, then with input $X$ and side information $X_r$. Averaging over $Q$ cannot increase either conditional mutual information, so both are bounded by the corresponding quantities under the averaged joint input law $P_{X,X_r}$. This gives the displayed maximum as an outer bound.

For achievability, view $(Y_r,Y)$ as the relay's observation and $Y$ as the destination output. This is a finite relay channel whose relay encoder can causally use the observation pair because it has full feedback in [F1]. Apply the block-Markov construction of [F3] with the relay observation $\widetilde Y_r=(Y_r,Y)$; its decoding term becomes $I(X;Y,Y_r|X_r)$, while the destination decoding term is $I(X,X_r;Y)$. Every joint input law factors as $P_{X_r}P_{X|X_r}$, so the construction achieves every rate below the displayed minimum.

The outer bound in step 1.1 and achievable rates in step 1.2 coincide for every joint input law. The joint-input probability simplex is compact. Each mutual information is continuous there because it is a finite sum of terms $-p\ln p$, with $p\ln p$ extended continuously by $0$ at $p=0$; the minimum of the two continuous functions is continuous. It therefore attains a maximum, and taking that maximum and closure proves the capacity formula.

citations.quote:
A **finite two-user interference channel** is the two-sender, two-receiver memoryless channel with finite nonempty input alphabets $\mathcal X_1,\mathcal X_2$, finite nonempty output alphabets $\mathcal Y_1,\mathcal Y_2$, and transition law $W(y_1,y_2|x_1,x_2)$. Independent uniform messages $M_1,M_2$ on finite nonempty sets are encoded separately as $X_1^n=f_1(M_1)$ and $X_2^n=f_2(M_2)$; receiver $i$ estimates $M_i$ from $Y_i^n$. The **strong-interference regime** means that, for every product law $P_{X_1}P_{X_2}$,
$$I(X_1;Y_1|X_2)\le I(X_1;Y_2|X_2),\qquad I(X_2;Y_2|X_1)\le I(X_2;Y_1|X_1).$$
The inequalities are evaluated under the stated product law and the channel. They are universal hypotheses over input laws, not just inequalities at a chosen optimizing distribution.

Assume the strong-interference inequalities of [[def-finite-two-user-interference-channel-and-strong-regime]]. For independent random vectors $X_1^n,X_2^n$, pass each coordinate through independent uses of the channel. Then
$$I(X_1^n;Y_1^n|X_2^n)\le I(X_1^n;Y_2^n|X_2^n),\qquad I(X_2^n;Y_2^n|X_1^n)\le I(X_2^n;Y_1^n|X_1^n).$$

Let $X$ take values in an alphabet $\mathcal X$ of size $m\ge2$, let $Y$ be finite, and let $\widehat X$ be an estimator in the same alphabet generated from $Y$, so the joint pmf factors as $p_{XY\widehat X}=p_{XY}p_{\widehat X|Y}$. Put $P_e=\mathbb P[\widehat X\ne X]$ and define

$$h_2(t):=-t\ln t-(1-t)\ln(1-t),\qquad 0\ln0:=0.$$

Then

$$H(X|Y)\le h_2(P_e)+P_e\ln(m-1)\le \ln2+P_e\ln m.$$

For $m=1$, $X$ is constant and $H(X|Y)=0$.

For the average-joint-error no-feedback code of [[def-it-two-user-discrete-memoryless-mac-code]] over the finite DM-MAC, the capacity region is the closure of the union over all finite $Q$ and laws $P_QP_{X_1|Q}P_{X_2|Q}W$ of
$$R_1\le I(X_1;Y\mid X_2,Q),\quad R_2\le I(X_2;Y\mid X_1,Q),\quad R_1+R_2\le I(X_1,X_2;Y\mid Q).$$
Here $Q$ is a public time-sharing variable independent of both private messages; conditional on each $Q=q$, the two input laws are a product. This result does not characterize maximal-error capacity.

For finite $X,Y,Z$ with a joint pmf,

$$H(X,Y|Z)=H(X|Z)+H(Y|X,Z),$$

and

$$I(X;Y,Z)=I(X;Z)+I(X;Y|Z).$$

In particular, $I(X;Y)=H(X)-H(X|Y)=H(Y)-H(Y|X)$. All terms are finite.

derivations.claim: For any length-$n$ code, independence of the messages makes the induced vectors $X_1^n,X_2^n$ independent. Fano at receiver 1 and the fact that revealing $M_2$ cannot reduce mutual information give $nR_1\le I(X_1^n;Y_1^n|X_2^n)+o(n)$. The analogous receiver-2 bound is $nR_2\le I(X_2^n;Y_2^n|X_1^n)+o(n)$.

Fix finite $Q$ and product conditional input laws. Apply [F4] to the marginal MAC at receiver 1 and to the marginal MAC at receiver 2. Both uses of [F4] generate the same ensemble of independent sender codebooks, because the input laws and time-sharing sequence are the same; only the two decoders differ. Under the strong-interference inequalities [F1], receiver 2's individual bound for sender 1 is at least receiver 1's intended individual bound, and receiver 1's individual bound for sender 2 is at least receiver 2's intended bound. The intersection of the two MAC regions is therefore exactly the three inequalities in the statement.

For the first individual bound, the finite entropy chain rule [F5] and memorylessness give $$I(X_1^n;Y_1^n|X_2^n)=H(Y_1^n|X_2^n)-H(Y_1^n|X_1^n,X_2^n)\le\sum_i I(X_{1,i};Y_{1,i}|X_{2,i}),$$ where the first entropy is at most $\sum_iH(Y_{1,i}|X_{2,i})$ by the chain rule and conditioning, and the second entropy is exactly $\sum_iH(Y_{1,i}|X_{1,i},X_{2,i})$ by the memoryless channel. The same calculation applies to user 2.

By the block-lift inequality [F2], $I(X_2^n;Y_1^n|X_1^n)\ge I(X_2^n;Y_2^n|X_1^n)$. Since $M_2$ is independent of $M_1$, Fano at receiver 2 implies $$H(M_2|Y_1^n,M_1)=H(M_2|M_1)-I(M_2;Y_1^n|M_1)\le H(M_2|M_1)-I(M_2;Y_2^n|M_1)=o(n).$$ Fano at receiver 1 gives $H(M_1|Y_1^n)=o(n)$. Thus $n(R_1+R_2)\le I(M_1,M_2;Y_1^n)+o(n)\le I(X_1^n,X_2^n;Y_1^n)+o(n)\le\sum_i I(X_{1,i},X_{2,i};Y_{1,i})+o(n)$. Exchanging receivers gives the corresponding sum bound at $Y_2$.

Let $Q$ be uniform on $[n]$ and let $(X_1,X_2)$ have the time-$Q$ input law; since the message vectors are independent, $P_{X_1,X_2|Q}=P_{X_1|Q}P_{X_2|Q}$. Combining steps 2.1, 2.2 gives the stated inequalities for this $Q$. Taking limits and closure proves the converse.

The [F4] random-coding proof gives ensemble-average error tending to zero at each receiver under the strict MAC inequalities. The expected sum of the two receiver errors is at most the sum of those two vanishing bounds, so a deterministic codebook pair exists for which both errors tend to zero. Closure removes strictness and the finite variable $Q$ supplies time sharing.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For the real or complex Gaussian interference channel of [[def-real-two-user-gaussian-interference-channel]], assume the strong regime
$$|h_{12}|\ge|h_{11}|,\qquad |h_{21}|\ge|h_{22}|.$$
Then the capacity region is the set of nonnegative rate pairs satisfying
$$R_1\le\kappa\log_2(1+\mathrm{SNR}_1),\quad R_2\le\kappa\log_2(1+\mathrm{SNR}_2),$$
$$R_1+R_2\le\kappa\min\{\log_2(1+\mathrm{SNR}_1+\mathrm{INR}_1),\log_2(1+\mathrm{SNR}_2+\mathrm{INR}_2)\},$$
where $\kappa=1/2$ for real and $1$ for complex channels.

The two-user Gaussian interference channel has independent messages, separate encoders, and outputs
$$Y_1=h_{11}X_1+h_{21}X_2+Z_1,\qquad Y_2=h_{12}X_1+h_{22}X_2+Z_2.$$
For the **real model**, $X_i,h_{ji},Z_j$ are real and $Z_j\sim N(0,1)$. For the **complex model**, the inputs and gains are complex and $Z_j\sim\mathcal{CN}(0,1)$ with density $\pi^{-1}e^{-|z|^2}$. The receiver-noise variables are independent across receivers and channel uses and independent of the messages, so the channel is memoryless. Each power budget satisfies $P_i\ge0$. A length-$n$ code has independent uniform messages $M_i$ on $[m_i]$ for integers $m_i\ge1$, deterministic separate encoders $X_i^n=f_i(M_i)$, and decoders $\widehat M_i=g_i(Y_i^n)$; no feedback is present. The expected average-power constraints are $n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^n\mathbb E[X_{i,t}^2]\le P_i$ in the real model and $n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^n\mathbb E|X_{i,t}|^2\le P_i$ in the complex model, with expectations under the uniform message law. The average joint error is $\Pr\{(\widehat M_1,\widehat M_2)\ne(M_1,M_2)\}$. For either model define
$$\mathrm{SNR}_1=|h_{11}|^2P_1,\quad \mathrm{SNR}_2=|h_{22}|^2P_2,\quad \mathrm{INR}_1=|h_{21}|^2P_2,\quad \mathrm{INR}_2=|h_{12}|^2P_1.$$
Rates are bits per use, $R_i=n^{-1}\log_2m_i$. For a scalar unit-noise AWGN link $Y=aX+Z$ with power constraint $P$, the capacity is $\kappa\log_2(1+|a|^2P)$, attained by a centered real Gaussian input or a circular complex Gaussian input; $\kappa=1/2$ in the real model and $\kappa=1$ in the complex model.

For either Gaussian model in [[def-real-two-user-gaussian-interference-channel]], choose private powers $0\le P_{1p},P_{2p}\le P_1,P_2$ and common powers $P_{ic}=P_i-P_{ip}$. Split each message into independent common and private parts, and transmit $X_i=U_i+V_i$ with independent centered Gaussian codewords of powers $P_{ic}$ and $P_{ip}$ (circular in the complex model). At receiver 1, decode $(U_1,V_1,U_2)$ and treat $V_2$ as Gaussian noise of variance $N_1=1+|h_{21}|^2P_{2p}$. At receiver 2, decode $(U_1,U_2,V_2)$ and treat $V_1$ as noise of variance $N_2=1+|h_{12}|^2P_{1p}$. A nonnegative rate split $R_i=R_{ic}+R_{ip}$ is achievable if, at each receiver $j$, every nonempty subset $T$ of its three decoded streams with positive total rate satisfies
$$\sum_{s\in T}R_s<\kappa\log_2\!\left(1+\frac{\sum_{s\in T}|a_{j,s}|^2P_s}{N_j}\right),$$
where $a_{1,1c}=a_{1,1p}=h_{11}$, $a_{1,2c}=h_{21}$, $a_{2,1c}=h_{12}$, and $a_{2,2c}=a_{2,2p}=h_{22}$; $\kappa=1/2$ for real and $1$ for complex channels. A zero-rate stream has a singleton message set and creates no false-message class; the all-zero split is always achievable. The closure of the union over feasible rate splits is an inner region.

For the complex Gaussian channel in [[def-real-two-user-gaussian-interference-channel]], the following are outer bounds in the listed regimes; all logarithms are base two. Write SNR and INR as defined there.

**Weak regime:** If $\mathrm{INR}_1<\mathrm{SNR}_2$ and $\mathrm{INR}_2<\mathrm{SNR}_1$, every achievable pair satisfies
$$R_1\le\log_2(1+\mathrm{SNR}_1),\quad R_2\le\log_2(1+\mathrm{SNR}_2),$$
$$R_1+R_2\le\log_2(1+\mathrm{SNR}_1)+\log_2\!\left(1+\frac{\mathrm{SNR}_2}{1+\mathrm{INR}_2}\right),$$
$$R_1+R_2\le\log_2(1+\mathrm{SNR}_2)+\log_2\!\left(1+\frac{\mathrm{SNR}_1}{1+\mathrm{INR}_1}\right),$$
$$R_1+R_2\le\log_2\!\left(1+\mathrm{INR}_1+\frac{\mathrm{SNR}_1}{1+\mathrm{INR}_2}\right)+\log_2\!\left(1+\mathrm{INR}_2+\frac{\mathrm{SNR}_2}{1+\mathrm{INR}_1}\right),$$
$$2R_1+R_2\le\log_2(1+\mathrm{SNR}_1+\mathrm{INR}_1)+\log_2\!\left(1+\mathrm{INR}_2+\frac{\mathrm{SNR}_2}{1+\mathrm{INR}_1}\right)+\log_2\!\left(\frac{1+\mathrm{SNR}_1}{1+\mathrm{INR}_2}\right),$$
$$R_1+2R_2\le\log_2(1+\mathrm{SNR}_2+\mathrm{INR}_2)+\log_2\!\left(1+\mathrm{INR}_1+\frac{\mathrm{SNR}_1}{1+\mathrm{INR}_2}\right)+\log_2\!\left(\frac{1+\mathrm{SNR}_2}{1+\mathrm{INR}_1}\right).$$

**Mixed regime:** If $\mathrm{INR}_1\ge\mathrm{SNR}_2$ and $\mathrm{INR}_2<\mathrm{SNR}_1$, every achievable pair satisfies the two individual bounds above and
$$R_1+R_2\le\log_2(1+\mathrm{SNR}_1)+\log_2\!\left(1+\frac{\mathrm{SNR}_2}{1+\mathrm{INR}_2}\right),\quad R_1+R_2\le\log_2(1+\mathrm{SNR}_1+\mathrm{INR}_1),$$
$$R_1+2R_2\le\log_2(1+\mathrm{SNR}_2+\mathrm{INR}_2)+\log_2\!\left(1+\mathrm{INR}_1+\frac{\mathrm{SNR}_1}{1+\mathrm{INR}_2}\right)+\log_2\!\left(1+\frac{\mathrm{SNR}_2}{1+\mathrm{INR}_1}\right).$$
The other mixed regime is obtained by interchanging user indices 1 and 2.

For the complex Gaussian channel in [[def-real-two-user-gaussian-interference-channel]], fix Gaussian common/private powers $P_{ic}+P_{ip}=P_i$, with each component nonnegative. Write $a=\mathrm{SNR}_1$, $b=\mathrm{SNR}_2$, $c=\mathrm{INR}_1$, $d=\mathrm{INR}_2$, $t_1=|h_{11}|^2P_{1p}$, $t_2=|h_{22}|^2P_{2p}$, $q_1=|h_{12}|^2P_{1p}$, $q_2=|h_{21}|^2P_{2p}$, $N_1=1+q_2$, $N_2=1+q_1$. All following logarithms are base two. Put
$$A_1=\log_2(1+t_1/N_1),\quad D_1=\log_2(1+a/N_1),\quad E_1=\log_2((1+c+t_1)/N_1),\quad G_1=\log_2((1+c+a)/N_1),$$
$$A_2=\log_2(1+t_2/N_2),\quad D_2=\log_2(1+b/N_2),\quad E_2=\log_2((1+d+t_2)/N_2),\quad G_2=\log_2((1+d+b)/N_2).$$
Every nonnegative pair satisfying
$$r_1\le D_1,\quad r_2\le D_2,$$
$$r_1+r_2\le A_1+G_2,\quad r_1+r_2\le A_2+G_1,\quad r_1+r_2\le E_1+E_2,$$
$$2r_1+r_2\le A_1+G_1+E_2,\quad r_1+2r_2\le A_2+G_2+E_1$$
is achievable by Gaussian superposition coding with the fixed split as a **nominal** distribution and with auxiliary removal and rate moving allowed. More precisely, if also $r_1\le A_1+E_2$ and $r_2\le A_2+E_1$, the original split suffices, with each receiver decoding its own message uniquely and the unintended common index nonuniquely. If the first extra inequality fails, one may discard user 2's private layer, encode all its information in its nominal common layer, encode all user 1 information in one full-power Gaussian codeword, let receiver 1 decode both codewords, and let receiver 2 treat user 1 as noise. The reflected alternative applies if the other extra inequality fails. The two extra inequalities cannot fail together. All codes satisfy the expected average power constraints. Closure includes singleton streams and boundary pairs.

Assume AC. Let $X$ be real or complex with finite second moment, let $Z$ be independent unit-variance Gaussian noise, and let $Y=aX+Z$. In the real case take $Z\sim N(0,1)$ and $a\in\mathbb R$; in the complex case take $Z\sim\mathcal{CN}(0,1)$ with density $\pi^{-1}e^{-|z|^2}$ and $a\in\mathbb C$. Put $v=\mathbb E|X-\mathbb EX|^2$ and $\kappa=1/2$ in the real case, $\kappa=1$ in the complex case. Then
$$I(X;Y)\le\kappa\ln(1+|a|^2v)\le\kappa\ln(1+|a|^2\mathbb E|X|^2)$$
in nats; division by $\ln2$ gives the corresponding bit formula.
Equality in the first inequality holds when $X$ is Gaussian in the real case or circular complex Gaussian in the complex case, including the zero-variance case.

derivations.claim: First suppose both prescribed powers are positive; zero powers are handled separately below. Write $a=\mathrm{SNR}_1$, $b=\mathrm{SNR}_2$, $c=\mathrm{INR}_1$, $d=\mathrm{INR}_2$ and $L(x)=\log_2 x$. The weak regime is $c<b$, $d<a$, the mixed regimes have exactly one reversed comparison, and the strong regime is $c\ge b$, $d\ge a$. Positive powers make these comparisons equivalent to the gain comparisons in [F1]. In the strong regime [F1] supplies the exact region, so there is no loss. We treat one mixed regime and obtain the other by exchanging all user indices.

In the weak regime set $k_c=\max(1,c)$, $k_d=\max(1,d)$, $q_1=\min(1,d)$, $q_2=\min(1,c)$, $t_1=a/k_d$, $t_2=b/k_c$, $N_1=1+q_2$, and $N_2=1+q_1$. These correspond to the nominal private powers $P_{1p}=P_1/k_d$ and $P_{2p}=P_2/k_c$, including zero cross gains without division by an INR. Let $A_i,D_i,E_i,G_i$ be [F5]'s quantities for this split. Then $1\le N_i\le2$, $t_1\ge a/(1+d)$, $t_2\ge b/(1+c)$, $(N_1+t_1)(1+d)\ge1+a$, and $(N_2+t_2)(1+c)\ge1+b$: for example $(1+d)/k_d\ge1$ and $N_1\ge1$. These elementary inequalities will compare all facets uniformly, including INR below one. Denote by $O_1,O_2,O_3$ the three weak outer sum right-hand sides in their displayed order and by $W_1,W_2$ the outer $2R_1+R_2$ and $R_1+2R_2$ right-hand sides.

In the mixed regime $c\ge b$, $d<a$, take $q_2=0$, $t_2=0$, $N_1=1$, $q_1=\min(1,d)$, $N_2=1+q_1$, $t_1=a/\max(1,d)$. Thus user 2 is nominally all common, and the private user 1 signal has unintended received power $\min(1,d)$. The seven-facet quantities become $A_1=L(1+t_1)$, $D_1=L(1+a)$, $E_1=L(1+c+t_1)$, $G_1=L(1+c+a)$, $A_2=0$, $D_2=L(1+b/N_2)$, $E_2=L((1+d)/N_2)$, and $G_2=L((1+d+b)/N_2)$. Let $O=L(1+a)+L(1+b/(1+d))$ and $V=L(1+b+d)+L(1+c+a/(1+d))+L(1+b/(1+c))$, the mixed outer first sum and weighted right sides. The remaining sum bound is $G_1$. Since $(1+d)/\max(1,d)\ge1$, we have $(1+t_1)(1+d)\ge1+a$ and $(1+c+t_1)(1+d)\ge1+c+a$.

It remains to justify clipping a coordinate at zero; a negative-coordinate polygon argument would not do this. If both capacity coordinates are at most one, use the zero code. Suppose $R_1\le1<R_2$ and write $B=L(1+b)$. The capacity individual bound gives $R_2\le B$, so it suffices to achieve $(0,\max(0,B-1))$ on the axis. Shut user 1 off. In a weak nominal split, if $c<1$ user 2 is entirely private and achieves $B$. If $c\ge1$, its desired private power is $b/c$ and its unintended private power is one. Its common layer can be decoded at the unintended receiver while treating its private layer as noise at any rate up to $C=L((1+c)/2)$. At its intended receiver the private rate bound is $A=L(1+b/c)$, the common bound is $H=L(1+b-b/c)$, and the total bound is $B$. The product identities $(1+b/c)(1+b-b/c)\ge1+b$ and $(1+b/c)(1+c)\ge1+b$ give $A+H\ge B$ and $A+C\ge B-1$. citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

A **real scalar Gaussian relay network** has node set $[N]$ for an integer $N\ge1$, source set $\mathcal S\subseteq[N]$, destination set $\mathcal D\subseteq[N]$, one real input $X_i$ and output $Y_i$ at each node, and channel equations
$$Y_j=\sum_{i=1}^N g_{ji}X_i+Z_j,\qquad j\in[N],$$
where the gains $g_{ji}\in\mathbb R$ are fixed and the noises $Z_j$ are independent $N(0,1)$ random variables, independent across channel uses and of all source messages. At each use the current noise vector is independent of all past observations and the current inputs; future inputs may depend on past noises through feedback. Each node has a nonnegative power budget $P_i\ge0$ and average power constraint $\frac1n\sum_{t=1}^n\mathbb E[X_{i,t}^2]\le P_i$. Each source $i\in\mathcal S$ has an independent uniform message $M_i$ in a finite nonempty set $\mathcal M_i$. For every non-source node $i\notin\mathcal S$, set $\mathcal M_i=\{*\}$ and $M_i=*$, so its encoder has no message information. A length-$n$ causal code uses measurable encoders $X_{i,t}=f_{i,t}(M_i,Y_i^{t-1})$ and destination decoders based on $(Y_d^n,M_d)$, where $M_d$ is its own source message when $d\in\mathcal S$ and a singleton otherwise; multicast means every destination must decode every other source message, while its own message is already known. The average error probability is the probability that any required destination estimate is wrong. Write $G_{B,A}$ for the matrix with rows indexed by $B$ and columns by $A$ whose entries are $g_{ji}$.

Rates in this page's Gaussian formulas are measured in bits per use, $R_i=n^{-1}\log_2|\mathcal M_i|$.

All mutual informations and rates in this item are measured in bits; differential entropies in the proof are in nats and are divided by $\ln2$.

In the real Gaussian multicast network of [[def-real-gaussian-multicast-relay-network]], take independent Gaussian inputs $X_i\sim N(0,P_i)$ and independent Gaussian test-channel noises. For a chosen node set $\mathcal Q\subseteq[N]$, set $\hat Y_i=Y_i+\hat Z_i$ with $\hat Z_i\sim N(0,1)$ for $i\in\mathcal Q$ and let $\hat Y_i$ be constant otherwise. Every nonnegative rate tuple satisfying
$$\sum_{k\in A\cap\mathcal S}R_k<I(X_A;Y_d,\hat Y_{A^c\cap\mathcal Q}\mid X_{A^c})-I(Y_{A\cap\mathcal Q};\hat Y_{A\cap\mathcal Q}\mid X_{[N]},Y_d,\hat Y_{A^c\cap\mathcal Q})$$
for every destination $d\in\mathcal D$ and every cut $A\subseteq[N]$ with $d\notin A$ and $A\cap\mathcal S\ne\varnothing$ is achievable under the stated average-power constraints. The closure of the union of these strict regions over the stated choices, together with the all-zero tuple, is achievable.

In the special case $P_i=P>0$ for every node and $\mathcal Q=[N]$, a noise-level evaluation gives the sufficient cut inequalities
$$\sum_{k\in A\cap\mathcal S}R_k < \frac12\log_2\det\!\left(I+\frac P2G(A)G(A)^T\right)-\frac{|A|}{2}$$
for every $A\subseteq[N]$ with $A^c\cap\mathcal D\ne\varnothing$ and $A\cap\mathcal S\ne\varnothing$, where $G(A)=G_{A^c,A}$. Their closure is achievable. The all-zero rate tuple is always achievable by singleton source-message sets, independently of whether these cut right-hand sides are nonnegative.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. If a random vector $X\in\mathbb R^d$ has a Lebesgue density, finite mean $m$, positive-definite covariance $K$, and finite differential entropy $h(X)=-\int f\ln f$, then
$$h(X)\le \frac12\ln\bigl((2\pi e)^d\det K\bigr).$$
Equality holds exactly when $X$ has the Gaussian law $N_d(m,K)$.

derivations.claim: Assume [A1] and use the independent unit-variance Gaussian inputs and quantizer noise stated in the example. For the cut separating the source alone, the relay sees $\sqrt{10}X+Z_r$, and adding independent unit-variance quantization noise makes total noise variance $2$. Thus the NNC first-cut mutual information is $\frac12\log_2(1+10/2)=\frac12\log_2 6$. The destination has no direct source term, so its observation adds zero information across this cut.

For the cut containing source and relay, the destination observes $\sqrt{10}X_r+Z_d$, so $I(X,X_r;Y_d)=\frac12\log_2(1+10)=\frac12\log_2 11$. Given all inputs and $Y_d$, the relay observation noise and independent quantization noise have variances $1$ and $1$, hence $I(Y_r;\hat Y_r|X,X_r,Y_d)=\frac12\log_2(2)=\frac12$. The two NNC cut rates are therefore the values in the minimum in the statement.

The first cut is larger because $6>11/2$ (equivalently $12>11$), so the minimum is $\frac12\log_2 11-\frac12$. In the cut-set expression, the source cut is $I(X;Y_r,Y_d|X_r)=I(X;Y_r|X_r)\le\frac12\log_2 11$ and the relay-to-destination cut is $I(X,X_r;Y_d)=I(X_r;Y_d)\le\frac12\log_2 11$, since the direct gain is zero; [F3] gives each Gaussian upper bound. Independent unit-power Gaussian inputs attain both terms, so the cut-set value is $\frac12\log_2 11$. Subtracting gives a gap of exactly $1/2$ bit.

The two-user Gaussian interference channel has independent messages, separate encoders, and outputs
$$Y_1=h_{11}X_1+h_{21}X_2+Z_1,\qquad Y_2=h_{12}X_1+h_{22}X_2+Z_2.$$
For the **real model**, $X_i,h_{ji},Z_j$ are real and $Z_j\sim N(0,1)$. For the **complex model**, the inputs and gains are complex and $Z_j\sim\mathcal{CN}(0,1)$ with density $\pi^{-1}e^{-|z|^2}$. The receiver-noise variables are independent across receivers and channel uses and independent of the messages, so the channel is memoryless. Each power budget satisfies $P_i\ge0$. A length-$n$ code has independent uniform messages $M_i$ on $[m_i]$ for integers $m_i\ge1$, deterministic separate encoders $X_i^n=f_i(M_i)$, and decoders $\widehat M_i=g_i(Y_i^n)$; no feedback is present. The expected average-power constraints are $n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^n\mathbb E[X_{i,t}^2]\le P_i$ in the real model and $n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^n\mathbb E|X_{i,t}|^2\le P_i$ in the complex model, with expectations under the uniform message law. The average joint error is $\Pr\{(\widehat M_1,\widehat M_2)\ne(M_1,M_2)\}$. For either model define
$$\mathrm{SNR}_1=|h_{11}|^2P_1,\quad \mathrm{SNR}_2=|h_{22}|^2P_2,\quad \mathrm{INR}_1=|h_{21}|^2P_2,\quad \mathrm{INR}_2=|h_{12}|^2P_1.$$
Rates are bits per use, $R_i=n^{-1}\log_2m_i$. For a scalar unit-noise AWGN link $Y=aX+Z$ with power constraint $P$, the capacity is $\kappa\log_2(1+|a|^2P)$, attained by a centered real Gaussian input or a circular complex Gaussian input; $\kappa=1/2$ in the real model and $\kappa=1$ in the complex model.

For the real or complex Gaussian interference channel of [[def-real-two-user-gaussian-interference-channel]], assume the strong regime
$$|h_{12}|\ge|h_{11}|,\qquad |h_{21}|\ge|h_{22}|.$$
Then the capacity region is the set of nonnegative rate pairs satisfying
$$R_1\le\kappa\log_2(1+\mathrm{SNR}_1),\quad R_2\le\kappa\log_2(1+\mathrm{SNR}_2),$$
$$R_1+R_2\le\kappa\min\{\log_2(1+\mathrm{SNR}_1+\mathrm{INR}_1),\log_2(1+\mathrm{SNR}_2+\mathrm{INR}_2)\},$$
where $\kappa=1/2$ for real and $1$ for complex channels.

A **finite two-user interference channel** is the two-sender, two-receiver memoryless channel with finite nonempty input alphabets $\mathcal X_1,\mathcal X_2$, finite nonempty output alphabets $\mathcal Y_1,\mathcal Y_2$, and transition law $W(y_1,y_2|x_1,x_2)$. Independent uniform messages $M_1,M_2$ on finite nonempty sets are encoded separately as $X_1^n=f_1(M_1)$ and $X_2^n=f_2(M_2)$; receiver $i$ estimates $M_i$ from $Y_i^n$. The **strong-interference regime** means that, for every product law $P_{X_1}P_{X_2}$,
$$I(X_1;Y_1|X_2)\le I(X_1;Y_2|X_2),\qquad I(X_2;Y_2|X_1)\le I(X_2;Y_1|X_1).$$
The inequalities are evaluated under the stated product law and the channel. They are universal hypotheses over input laws, not just inequalities at a chosen optimizing distribution.

For the channel and universal strong-interference assumptions of [[def-finite-two-user-interference-channel-and-strong-regime]], the capacity region is the closure of the union over finite $Q$ and laws $P_QP_{X_1|Q}P_{X_2|Q}$ of rate pairs satisfying
$$R_1\le I(X_1;Y_1|X_2,Q),\quad R_2\le I(X_2;Y_2|X_1,Q),$$
$$R_1+R_2\le \min\{I(X_1,X_2;Y_1|Q),I(X_1,X_2;Y_2|Q)\}.$$

Each receiver observes its own input noiselessly. A binary code of rate below one can therefore be sent independently by each user. Since each output alphabet has size two, no rate can exceed one bit per use. Taking closure gives the true capacity square.

For every finite time-sharing variable $Q$ and every conditional product input law, each output is binary, so $I_2(X_1,X_2;Y_i|Q)\le H_2(Y_i|Q)\le1$. Consequently every rate pair in the entire union and its closure asserted by the formula in [F2] satisfies $R_1+R_2\le1$ bit per use. This excludes $(1,1)$, which step 1.2 places in the true capacity square. Hence the formula without the strong-interference hypothesis is false.

A **finite two-user interference channel** is the two-sender, two-receiver memoryless channel with finite nonempty input alphabets $\mathcal X_1,\mathcal X_2$, finite nonempty output alphabets $\mathcal Y_1,\mathcal Y_2$, and transition law $W(y_1,y_2|x_1,x_2)$. Independent uniform messages $M_1,M_2$ on finite nonempty sets are encoded separately as $X_1^n=f_1(M_1)$ and $X_2^n=f_2(M_2)$; receiver $i$ estimates $M_i$ from $Y_i^n$. The **strong-interference regime** means that, for every product law $P_{X_1}P_{X_2}$,
$$I(X_1;Y_1|X_2)\le I(X_1;Y_2|X_2),\qquad I(X_2;Y_2|X_1)\le I(X_2;Y_1|X_1).$$
The inequalities are evaluated under the stated product law and the channel. They are universal hypotheses over input laws, not just inequalities at a chosen optimizing distribution.

For the channel and universal strong-interference assumptions of [[def-finite-two-user-interference-channel-and-strong-regime]], the capacity region is the closure of the union over finite $Q$ and laws $P_QP_{X_1|Q}P_{X_2|Q}$ of rate pairs satisfying
$$R_1\le I(X_1;Y_1|X_2,Q),\quad R_2\le I(X_2;Y_2|X_1,Q),$$
$$R_1+R_2\le \min\{I(X_1,X_2;Y_1|Q),I(X_1,X_2;Y_2|Q)\}.$$

derivations.claim: For every product input law, conditioning on $X_2$ makes both $Y_1$ and $Y_2$ equal to $X_1$ plus the same fixed bit; hence $I_2(X_1;Y_1|X_2)=I_2(X_1;Y_2|X_2)$. Conditioning on $X_1$ gives $I_2(X_2;Y_2|X_1)=I_2(X_2;Y_1|X_1)$. Thus [F1] holds with equality.

Each receiver's output is one bit, so its multiple-access sum mutual information is at most $H_2(Y_i)\le1$. Also, given the other input, each user sees a noiseless binary channel, whose mutual information is at most one bit. Therefore the region in [F2] is contained in the stated triangle.

With independent uniform inputs, $Y_i$ is uniform, and $I_2(X_1;Y_1|X_2)=I_2(X_2;Y_2|X_1)=I_2(X_1,X_2;Y_i)=1$. The MAC intersection contains the two corner points $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$; the zero pair is achieved by singleton messages. Time sharing among these three points achieves every nonnegative pair with sum at most one. Together with step 1.2 this proves the capacity region.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

A **finite discrete memoryless network (DMN)** has a node set $[N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ for an integer $N\ge1$, finite nonempty input alphabets $\mathcal X_k$ and output alphabets $\mathcal Y_k$, and one transition probability vector $W(y_1,\ldots,y_N\mid x_1,\ldots,x_N)$ for each input tuple. At each use, conditional on the current input tuple, the output tuple is drawn from this vector independently of earlier uses.

Node $k$ may have an independent uniform message $M_k$ in a finite nonempty set $\mathcal M_k$ and a destination set $D_k\subseteq[N]$. A length-$n$ **causal code** consists of encoders $X_{k,i}=f_{k,i}(M_k,Y_k^{i-1})$ and, for each destination $d\in D_k$, a decoder $\widehat M_{kd}=g_{kd}(Y_d^n,M_d)$; here $Y_k^{i-1}=(Y_{k,1},\ldots,Y_{k,i-1})$, with the empty tuple at $i=1$. The average error is the probability that any required estimate differs from its message. A rate tuple is achievable if a sequence of such codes has error tending to zero and message-set rates tending to at least that tuple; the capacity region is the closure of achievable tuples.

Let $p_{XYZ}$ be a joint probability vector on finite alphabets and write $p_Z(z)$ for its marginal. It is the law of finite coordinate random elements on the canonical finite probability space from [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]] and [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]. For each $z$ with $p_Z(z)>0$, the conditional law $p_{XY|z}$ and its marginals $p_{X|z},p_{Y|z}$ are probability vectors by [[lem-it-finite-marginals-and-conditionals-are-pmfs]]. Define conditional mutual information in nats by

$$I(X;Y|Z):=\sum_{z:p_Z(z)>0}p_Z(z)D(p_{XY|z}\|p_{X|z}\otimes p_{Y|z}),$$

using the finite KL convention of [[def-qa-35-finite-probability-entropy-and-stochastic-matrices]], where $(p_{X|z}\otimes p_{Y|z})(x,y):=p_{X|z}(x)p_{Y|z}(y)$. A positive conditional joint mass forces both conditional marginals to be positive, so each displayed KL term is finite. Zero-mass conditioning values contribute no term. The base-$b$ version replaces $\ln$ by $\log_b$ inside the conditional KL sums.

For finite $X,Y,Z$,

$$I(X;Y|Z)=H(X|Z)+H(Y|Z)-H(X,Y|Z)\ge0.$$

Equality holds if and only if, for every $z$ with $p_Z(z)>0$, the conditional joint pmf factors as $p_{XY|z}=p_{X|z}p_{Y|z}$; this is conditional independence given $Z$.

For finite $X,Y,Z$ with a joint pmf,

$$H(X,Y|Z)=H(X|Z)+H(Y|X,Z),$$

and

$$I(X;Y,Z)=I(X;Z)+I(X;Y|Z).$$

In particular, $I(X;Y)=H(X)-H(X|Y)=H(Y)-H(Y|X)$. All terms are finite.

Assume AC. Let $U,V,Y,S$ take values in standard-Borel spaces. Then
$$I((U,V);Y|S)=I(U;Y|S)+I(V;Y|U,S)$$
and also
$$I((U,V);Y|S)=I(V;Y|S)+I(U;Y|V,S),$$
where these are equalities of extended nonnegative quantities. In particular, if the conditional law of $Y$ given $(U,V,S)$ depends only on $(V,S)$, then
$$I(U;Y|S)\le I(V;Y|S).$$

Let $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ be IID square-integrable real random variables, with $\mu=\mathbb EX_1$ and $\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(X_1)$. For $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nX_k$,
$$\mathbb E|S_n/n-\mu|^2=\sigma^2/n,$$
and $S_n/n\to\mu$ in $L^2$ and in probability. Also $\mathbb P(|S_n/n-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)\le\sigma^2/(n\varepsilon^2)$ for $\varepsilon>0$.

derivations.claim: Write $C_k=I(Y_k;\hat Y_k|X_k,Q)$. Fix $a>0$ and $0<\epsilon<1/2$. Choose a deterministic word $q^n$ whose symbol proportions tend to $P_Q$, omitting zero-probability symbols. For node $k$ let $r_k^n(du|x,y)=\prod_tP_{\hat Y_k|X_k,Y_k,q_t}(du_t|x_t,y_t)$ and $\mu_k^n(du|x)=\prod_tP_{\hat Y_k|X_k,q_t}(du_t|x_t)$. Define $H_k(x,y)=\{u:\log(dr_k^n/d\mu_k^n)(u)\le n(C_k+a)\}$ and $Z_k(x,y)=r_k^n(H_k|x,y)$. Under the target product law, the information density is a sum of the stated square-integrable local log likelihoods. Apply [F4] separately to the finitely many positive-probability $q$ subblocks; their lengths tend to infinity and their proportions tend to $P_Q$. Thus its normalized sum tends in probability to $C_k$, so $\mathbb E(1-Z_k)\to0$. The pointwise inequality $\mathbf1_{\{1-Z_k>\epsilon\}}\le(1-Z_k)/\epsilon$ shows that pairs with $Z_k<1-\epsilon$ have probability tending to zero.

For a good pair $Z_k\ge1-\epsilon$, put $T_k=r_k^n\mathbf1_{H_k}/Z_k$ and $M_k=e^{n(C_k+a)}/(1-\epsilon)$. Generate $L_k=\lceil e^{n\rho_k}\rceil$ independent reconstruction entries with law $\mu_k^n$, where $\rho_k>C_k+a$. Test entries in order, accepting $u$ with probability $(dT_k/d\mu_k^n)(u)/M_k$ using an independent uniform for each entry. This is at most one, its mean is $p_k=1/M_k$, and $p_k$ is independent of the good pair. The no-acceptance probability is $(1-p_k)^{L_k}\le e^{-L_k/M_k}\to0$. Use a fixed default index on a bad pair or no acceptance. Conditional on acceptance at a specified label $\ell$, the accepted entry has law $T_k$; an earlier rejected entry has law $\mu_k^n(du|x)(1-(dT_k/d\mu_k^n)(u)/M_k)/(1-p_k)$, bounded by $2\mu_k^n$ for large $n$; later entries retain law $\mu_k^n$. Multiplication of the independent entry and uniform densities proves these statements and conditional independence of the entries given the pair and $\ell$.

Since $T_k\le r_k^n/(1-\epsilon)$ and $\|T_k-r_k^n\|_{\rm TV}=1-Z_k$ on good pairs, the averaged total variation error of the selected reconstruction kernel tends to zero by step 1.1. Summing these errors over the finitely many nodes compares their product kernels to the target product test channel; the bound follows by replacing one kernel at a time and integrating bounded indicator functions. Consequently every full-tuple target event of probability tending to one also holds with probability tending to one for the selected reconstructions, apart from the already vanishing selection failures. Draw one independent uniform for each node, block, message, previous-index branch, and reconstruction entry. A transmitted branch exposes each such uniform at most once. Uninspected branches retain their independent codewords and uniforms; the finite array will be fixed at the end.

Set $J_d(A,U)=\sum_qP_Q(q)D(P_{d,q}\|Q_{d,A,U,q})$. The block acceptance test at destination $d$ is the intersection, over every allowed $(A,U)$, of $\log\frac{d\prod_tP_{d,q_t}}{d\prod_tQ_{d,A,U,q_t}}(v^n)\ge n(J_d(A,U)-a).$ By the square-integrability hypothesis and [F4], all these finitely many tests accept the true target block with probability tending to one. On the displayed event the reference product measure is at most $e^{-n(J_d(A,U)-a)}$ times the target product measure; integration therefore bounds its reference probability by $e^{-n(J_d(A,U)-a)}$. This argument applies to discrete sums and Euclidean integrals alike.

Let $E_d(A)=J_d(A,\varnothing)$. Conditional KL chain rules, using independence of the inputs given $Q$, give $E_d(A)=I(X_A;\hat Y_{A^c},Y_d|X_{A^c},Q)+\sum_{k\in A}I(\hat Y_k;X_{[N]},\hat Y_{A^c},Y_d,\hat Y_{\{j\in A:j<k\}}|X_k,Q).$ For a direct verification in finite alphabets, expand the reference likelihood: the input contribution is $\sum_{k\in A}H(X_k|Q)-H(X_A|X_{A^c},\hat Y_{A^c},Y_d,Q)$, and the reconstruction contribution is $\sum_{k\in A}H(\hat Y_k|X_k,Q)-H(\hat Y_A|X_{[N]},\hat Y_{A^c},Y_d,Q)$; order the latter entropy by $k$. The conditional-KL expansion gives the identical formula in the Euclidean case without assuming finite differential entropy. A further chain expansion shows that $J_d(A,U)-E_d(A)$ is the conditional KL of $P_{\hat Y_U|X_{A^c},\hat Y_{(A\cup U)^c},Y_d,Q}$ from $\prod_{k\in U}P_{\hat Y_k|X_k,Q}$, averaged over the displayed conditioning tuple. It is nonnegative; in finite entropy notation it equals $\sum_{k\in U}H(\hat Y_k|X_k,Q)-H(\hat Y_U|X_{A^c},\hat Y_{(A\cup U)^c},Y_d,Q)$. Thus $J_d(A,U)\ge E_d(A)$ for every wrong-current-index pattern.

Subtract $C_k$ from the $k$th reconstruction summand in step 5.1. The test-channel factorization says that given $X_{[N]},Y_A,Q$, the reconstructions in $A$ are conditionally independent and depend only on their own $(X_k,Y_k,Q)$. In finite entropy notation the sum of differences is therefore $H(\hat Y_A|X_{[N]},Y_A,\hat Y_{A^c},Y_d,Q)-H(\hat Y_A|X_{[N]},\hat Y_{A^c},Y_d,Q)$; conditional-KL chain expansion gives the same identity for the assumed finite Euclidean informations. Consequently $E_d(A)-\sum_{k\in A}C_k=I(X_A;\hat Y_{A^c},Y_d|X_{A^c},Q)-I(Y_A;\hat Y_A|X_{[N]},\hat Y_{A^c},Y_d,Q)=F_d(A).$ This cancellation uses the product test channels and does not require independent channel outputs.

For each constrained node with a strict mean-cost inequality choose $\mathbb E c_k(X_k)<\Gamma_k'<\Gamma_k$, and condition each independent product input word on $\sum_tc_k(x_{k,t})\le n\Gamma_k'$. Its conditioning probability $b_{k,n}$ tends to one by [F4], since the cost has finite second moment; the finite-$Q$ subblock argument of step 1.1 applies. Each such word obeys the cost bound deterministically. Its law has density at most $1/b_{k,n}$ relative to the target product input law and total variation distance $1-b_{k,n}$. At an unconstrained node use the unconditioned word and put $b_{k,n}=1$; at a deterministic already-feasible constrained node use its fixed word and also put $b_{k,n}=1$, so no strict slack is needed there. For a fresh block the transmitted input tuple is within $\sum_k(1-b_{k,n})$ of its target product law, uniformly in all previous labels. Passing through a kernel preserves this upper bound, because an event's conditional probability is in $[0,1]$. Thus the vanishing selection-failure and true-test estimates remain valid for these input words.

Choose a fixed block count $B$. At node $k$ in each block $j$, independently generate $X_{k,j}(m,l)$ for $1\le m\le\lfloor e^{nBr_k}\rfloor$ and $1\le l\le L_k$, using singleton messages when $r_k=0$ or $k\notin\mathcal S$, and the word law from step 7.1. For each word generate $L_k$ reconstruction words from $\mu_k^n(\cdot|X_{k,j}(m,l))$ and the uniforms of step 3.1. All nodes, branches and blocks are independent. Initialize $l_{k,0}=1$. In block $j$ send $X_{k,j}(m_k,l_{k,j-1})$, and after the block choose $l_{k,j}$ by step 2.1. This is causal. A destination fixes its own message and its own actual index sequence, and selects the unique other-source message tuple for which some remaining index sequence passes every block test from step 4.1. Ties or no tuple are errors; compression indices need not be uniquely decoded. Every operation is a finite search through measurable tests. The message is repeated across all $B$ blocks, so length $nB$ gives rate tending to $r_k$.

The exact unnormalized measure for one true block and specified successful labels is $\left(\prod_k(1-p_k)^{\ell_k-1}p_k\right)\mathbf1_G(x,y)\left(\prod_k\mu_{X_k,n}(dx_k)\right)W^{\otimes n}(dy|x)\prod_kT_k(du_k|x_k,y_k),$ where $G$ means every local pair is good and $\mu_{X_k,n}$ is the word law. There is no division by $\Pr(G)$. Integrate nuisance true coordinates and use step 9.1. At most two input words per node are exposed, each bounded by $1/b_{k,n}\le2$ for large $n$. The candidate block subprobability is therefore bounded by the geometric label weight times $K\prod_tQ_{d,A_j,U_j,q_t}$, with $K=2^{3N}(1-\epsilon)^{-N}$ independent of all labels and $n$. Retaining the indicator $\mathbf1_G\le1$ can only reduce this bound. For a fixed true path, different block arrays are independent; all its branch labels are fixed. The sum of its geometric weights over allowed true paths is at most one. Thus the block packing bounds multiply, with no conditioning on a possibly rare global good event.

Drop the first block's false-message test. For each remaining block step 4.1 and $J_d(A_j,U_j)\ge E_d(A_j)$ give the factor $K e^{-n(E_d(A_j)-a)}$, independently of $U_j$. For a fixed previous-index pattern $A$, at most $\prod_{k\in A}L_k$ previous-index vectors realize it; at most $2^{N-1}$ sets $A$ contain $T$ and exclude $d$. There are at most $\prod_{k

If constrained cuts exist, their finitely many strict rate gaps have a positive minimum $g$. Choose $a$ small and then $\rho_k>C_k+a$ with $\rho_k-C_k$ small enough that $\sum_{k\in A}(\rho_k-C_k)+a<g/2$ on every cut. Step 6.1 gives $E_d(A)-\rho(A)=F_d(A)-\sum_{k\in A}(\rho_k-C_k)$. For every $A\supseteq T$, nonnegativity gives $r(T)\le r(A\cap\mathcal S)<F_d(A)$. Choose $B$ sufficiently large that $r(T)<\frac{B-1}{B}\min_{T\subseteq A,\ d\notin A}\{E_d(A)-\rho(A)-a\}-\frac1B\sum_{k\ne d}\rho_k$ for all finitely many $T,d$. This is possible because the remaining strict gaps are at least $g/2$. Fix those choices and let $n\to\infty$. Every exponential term in step 11.1 tends to zero, as do the true-message failures. If no constrained cuts exist, all required messages are either absent or already known locally and there is nothing to decode. A finite union over destinations proves multicast reliability.

In the finite branch, every fixed codebook and seed array induces one of finitely many deterministic encoder/decoder functions on the finite message and observation domains. Aggregate the ensemble distribution over this finite set of functions, enumerate it, and take the first code whose error is at most the ensemble average. Thus neither the auxiliary uniforms nor selection of the final finite code assumes AC. In the Euclidean branch average error over codebooks, messages and the finite uniform arrays and select a deterministic realization whose error tends to zero; a realization of error at most twice the positive average exists by integration, while if the average is zero almost every realization has zero error. The fixed-seed encoders and decoders remain measurable and causal. Each chosen input word obeys its shell bound, so concatenating $B$ words gives the claimed pointwise and expected costs; no random ensemble power assertion is used to select the deterministic code. Constant reconstructions contribute zero information and satisfy the same construction. The all-zero tuple uses singleton messages and any allowed fixed inputs, with zero error. Finally choose strict-region tuples tending to any point of the closure and, for the $j$th tuple, a sufficiently long code of error below $1/j$ and rate within $1/j$ of that tuple. These codes realize the closure by the definition of achievability.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The two-user Gaussian interference channel has independent messages, separate encoders, and outputs
$$Y_1=h_{11}X_1+h_{21}X_2+Z_1,\qquad Y_2=h_{12}X_1+h_{22}X_2+Z_2.$$
For the **real model**, $X_i,h_{ji},Z_j$ are real and $Z_j\sim N(0,1)$. For the **complex model**, the inputs and gains are complex and $Z_j\sim\mathcal{CN}(0,1)$ with density $\pi^{-1}e^{-|z|^2}$. The receiver-noise variables are independent across receivers and channel uses and independent of the messages, so the channel is memoryless. Each power budget satisfies $P_i\ge0$. A length-$n$ code has independent uniform messages $M_i$ on $[m_i]$ for integers $m_i\ge1$, deterministic separate encoders $X_i^n=f_i(M_i)$, and decoders $\widehat M_i=g_i(Y_i^n)$; no feedback is present. The expected average-power constraints are $n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^n\mathbb E[X_{i,t}^2]\le P_i$ in the real model and $n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^n\mathbb E|X_{i,t}|^2\le P_i$ in the complex model, with expectations under the uniform message law. The average joint error is $\Pr\{(\widehat M_1,\widehat M_2)\ne(M_1,M_2)\}$. For either model define
$$\mathrm{SNR}_1=|h_{11}|^2P_1,\quad \mathrm{SNR}_2=|h_{22}|^2P_2,\quad \mathrm{INR}_1=|h_{21}|^2P_2,\quad \mathrm{INR}_2=|h_{12}|^2P_1.$$
Rates are bits per use, $R_i=n^{-1}\log_2m_i$. For a scalar unit-noise AWGN link $Y=aX+Z$ with power constraint $P$, the capacity is $\kappa\log_2(1+|a|^2P)$, attained by a centered real Gaussian input or a circular complex Gaussian input; $\kappa=1/2$ in the real model and $\kappa=1$ in the complex model.

Assume AC. Let $Z\in\mathbb C$ have a Lebesgue density, finite mean $\mu$, finite differential entropy, and positive-definite real covariance matrix $K$ for $(\operatorname{Re}Z,\operatorname{Im}Z)$. Put $\sigma^2=\mathbb E|Z-\mu|^2=\operatorname{tr}K$. Then
$$h(Z)\le\ln(\pi e\sigma^2).$$
Equality holds exactly for the circular complex Gaussian law $\mathcal{CN}(\mu,\sigma^2)$ with density $(\pi\sigma^2)^{-1}\exp(-|z-\mu|^2/\sigma^2)$.

Let $f$ be a Lebesgue probability density on $\mathbb R^d$ with $\|f\|_\infty<\infty$ and $\int |x|^2f(x)\,dx<\infty$. Then $\int f(x)|\ln f(x)|\,dx<\infty$, so the differential entropy in [[def-it-real-differential-entropy]] is a finite real number.

Assume AC. Let $U,V,Y,S$ take values in standard-Borel spaces. Then
$$I((U,V);Y|S)=I(U;Y|S)+I(V;Y|U,S)$$
and also
$$I((U,V);Y|S)=I(V;Y|S)+I(U;Y|V,S),$$
where these are equalities of extended nonnegative quantities. In particular, if the conditional law of $Y$ given $(U,V,S)$ depends only on $(V,S)$, then
$$I(U;Y|S)\le I(V;Y|S).$$

Let $(E,\mathcal E)$ and $(F,\mathcal F)$ be measurable spaces and let $P$ be a probability measure on $(E\times F,\mathcal E\otimes\mathcal F)$. Its marginals are $P_E(A)=P(A\times F)$ and $P_F(B)=P(E\times B)$. The product probability $P_E\otimes P_F$ exists by the finite product-measure theorem. For the absolutely continuous branch $P\ll P_E\otimes P_F$, assume AC as required by [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]; the non-absolutely-continuous branch below remains $+\infty$. Define the **measure-theoretic mutual information** of the joint law $P$ by
$$I(P):=D(P\|P_E\otimes P_F)\in[0,+\infty].$$
For random elements $X,Y$ with joint law $P_{XY}$, write $I(X;Y):=I(P_{XY})$. The logarithm convention is the natural logarithm, so finite values are in nats as fixed by [[def-it-information-units-and-logarithm-base]]. The divergence is directional in its two law arguments and is $+\infty$ when $P_{XY}\not\ll P_X\otimes P_Y$.

This definition uses only the joint law, not a choice of density or a difference of entropy quantities.

derivations.claim: If $(T,S)$ are jointly Gaussian-smoothed finite-second-moment scalar variables with nonsingular joint Gaussian noise, then $h(T|S)=h(T-kS|S)\le h(T-kS)\le\log_2(\pi e\operatorname{Var}(T-kS))$ for every complex $k$. The first identity is conditional translation and the first inequality is conditional mutual-information nonnegativity; the second is [F2]. A finite-dimensional convolution with a nonsingular Gaussian has a bounded density, finite second moment, and positive-definite real covariance; [F3], applied after identifying complex vectors with real vectors, therefore makes every relevant joint, marginal, and residual differential entropy finite and verifies the hypotheses of [F2]. In particular the pairs $(Y_1^n,S_1^n)$ and $(Y_2^n,S_2^n)$ have nonsingular independent receiver-noise coordinates, and the degraded pair below has nonsingular joint Gaussian noise when $s>t$. Their conditional entropies are differences of these finite joint and marginal entropies. For conditioning additionally on $X_1^n$, which need not have a density, first subtract its known translated contribution; independence removes that conditioning and leaves the nonsingular smoothed pair $(h_{22}X_2^n+Z_2^n,S_2^n)$. For a channel with conditional density $w(t|x)$ and positive output density $f_T(t)$, the joint-to-product density ratio is $w(t|x)/f_T(t)$. Thus [F5] gives $I(X;T)=\int\ln(w(t|x)/f_T(t))\,dP_{X,T}$. When $T=BX+Z$ with independent nonsingular Gaussian $Z$, the two log integrals are finite by [F3] and the quadratic Gaussian log density, and this integral equals $(\ln 2)[h(T)-h(Z)]$. The same calculation with conditional densities justifies the conditional entropy identities used below, with every base-two entropy difference equal to the corresponding mutual information divided by $\ln 2$, since their joint and marginal entropies are finite as established above. At zero signal power the same Gaussian density argument applies without alteration. Coordinate entropy chain rules give $h(T^n|S^n)\le\sum_j h(T_j|S_j)$.

Suppose $s>t$ and set $U^n=\sqrt{s}X^n+Z^n$, $V^n=\sqrt{t/s}\,U^n+\sqrt{1-t/s}\,W^n$. The marginal law of $V^n$ is the lower-SNR channel and $X^n-U^n-V^n$ is Markov. The chain rule and step 1.1 give $h(U^n)-h(V^n)=[I(X^n;U^n)-I(X^n;V^n)]/\ln 2=I(X^n;U^n|V^n)/\ln 2=h(U^n|V^n)-n\log_2(\pi e[1-t/s])$: the conditional noise is $Z^n$ given $\sqrt{t/s}Z^n+\sqrt{1-t/s}W^n$. For a coordinate variance $p_j$, minimizing the quadratic residual variance of $U_j$ given $V_j$ gives $(1-t/s)(1+sp_j)/(1+tp_j)$. Step 1.1 therefore bounds the entropy difference by $\sum_j\log_2((1+sp_j)/(1+tp_j))$. This logarithmic ratio has derivative $(s-t)/((1+sp)(1+tp)\ln2)$, which is nonnegative and decreasing. Jensen and the average variance bound yield the first claimed inequality. If $s=t$ the two marginal entropies agree; if $t=0<s$ the same construction and computation apply. If $s=t=0$ both outputs are pure Gaussian noise.

Let $p_{i,j}=\operatorname{Var}(X_{i,j})$. The optimal scalar linear estimate of $Y_{1,j}$ from $S_{1,j}$ has residual variance $1+|h_{21}|^2p_{2,j}+|h_{11}|^2p_{1,j}/(1+|h_{12}|^2p_{1,j})$: independence of the two user vectors and the noises eliminates all other covariances. Step 1.1 bounds the conditional entropy by the logarithm of this variance times $\pi e$. The map $x\mapsto x/(1+kx)$ is increasing and concave on $[0,\infty)$ for $k\ge0$, with second derivative $-2k/(1+kx)^3$; hence the residual variance is increasing and concave in the two powers, and its logarithm is also concave and increasing. Jensen and $n^{-1}\sum_jp_{i,j}\le P_i$ give the first conditional-output bound. Reflection gives the second. This calculation has no division by a channel gain and remains valid when any gain vanishes.

The output variances are $1+|h_{11}|^2p_{1,j}+|h_{21}|^2p_{2,j}$ and $1+|h_{12}|^2p_{1,j}+|h_{22}|^2p_{2,j}$. Applying the coordinate chain rule, [F2], and logarithmic Jensen gives the two unconditioned-output bounds. Given $X_1^n$, subtract its contribution from $Y_2^n$; independence leaves the linear-estimation problem for $h_{22}X_2^n+Z_2^n$ from $h_{21}X_2^n+Z_1^n$. Its coordinate residual variance is $1+|h_{22}|^2p_{2,j}/(1+|h_{21}|^2p_{2,j})$. The same concavity calculation proves the final conditional bound. Reflection proves its counterpart.
